harder.updated_question: Example of underreporting of race/ethnicity data in research studies regardless of all the policies requiring race/ethnicity data
harder.verification_criterion: The answer provides at least one specific, documented example of a research study or set of studies where race/ethnicity data was underreported despite existing policies requiring such data collection.

attempts.answer:
Below are concrete, documented examples of underreporting and poor standardization of race/ethnicity in research despite existing mandates, along with analyses of why it persists and what the consequences are.

Why underreporting persists despite mandates
- Policy coverage and heterogeneity: Multiple U.S. policies since the 1990s require collection and reporting of race/ethnicity for NIH-funded studies, FDA-regulated trials, and public health surveillance, yet compliance and enforcement remain inconsistent across sponsors, institutions, and countries, with variations in definitions and collection procedures contributing to incomplete or nonstandardized data <cite id="4d23abfe-1">Various policies and guidelines have been issued regarding the reporting of race and ethnicity data for the U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH)-funded trial participants since the 1990s; in 2016, the NIH introduced a final rule mandating that demographic characteristics, including race and ethnicity, be reported in ClinicalTrials.gov; despite these policies and guidelines, reporting remains insufficient with inconsistent enforcement and compliance, with variations in race/ethnicity definitions and collection across studies</cite>. 
- Sponsor/institutional capacity and incentives: Sponsors and research teams may lack accountability resources or face misalignment of incentives, and data security/privacy concerns can deter disclosure of sensitive identity attributes like race/ethnicity, further reducing reporting; observational studies are less likely than interventional trials to report race/ethnicity even when data are available <cite id="4d23abfe-1">some sponsors and researchers may lack accountability or resources to adhere strictly to reporting standards; trial participants may be reluctant to disclose sensitive personal information, including race and ethnicity data, given data security and privacy concerns</cite> <cite id="4d23abfe-0">Across all study years, observational studies were consistently less likely than interventional trials to report race, ethnicity, or both</cite>.
- Cross-national variation and language resources: International trials face multilingual and cross-country differences in racial/ethnic classification, contributing to underreporting and misalignment with U.S. standards; these issues are visible in the underrepresentation of Asian groups in global trials registered in ClinicalTrials.gov despite their prevalence in the U.S. and worldwide <cite id="4d23abfe-0">the availability of multilingual recruitment and reporting resources is critical to diversity initiatives; the low and declining percentage of Asian and other racial groups is concerning, especially considering the large prevalence of Asian individuals in the US and globally</cite>.
- Enforcement gaps and delayed/omitted subgroup analyses: Even when policies exist, major reports have omitted or delayed reporting of outcomes by race/ethnicity and collapsed multiple minority groups into a single category, undermining the intent of mandates and masking group-specific effects, as seen in COVID-19 analyses <cite id="4d23abfe-3">Major research reports often omit or delay reporting demographics and outcomes by subpopulation, contravening NIH requirements; a trial investigating dexamethasone delayed reporting outcomes by race/ethnicity; in a separate report evaluating hydroxychloroquine, all racial/ethnic minorities were grouped into a singular population, despite evidence of group-specific differences</cite>.

Concrete examples and magnitudes across study types
- Clinical trials and trial registries: A 2009–2024 analysis of ClinicalTrials.gov shows that while reporting has improved, in 2024 about one in five studies still provided no race/ethnicity data (17.2%) and nearly one-third reported only race or only ethnicity (28.2%); categories were skewed toward “White” and “Not Hispanic or Latino,” and did not align with Census distributions, indicating both underreporting and misclassification risks <cite id="4d23abfe-4">In 2024, 17.2% of studies still did not report any data on race and ethnicity, and 28.2% only reported either race or ethnicity; “Not Hispanic or Latino” and “White” were the most common categories across time, with the breakdown of race and ethnicity categories not aligning with Census data across time</cite>. Earlier, more than half of registered studies had failed to report race/ethnicity by the late 2000s, and observational studies were persistently less likely than interventional trials to report these demographics <cite id="4d23abfe-0">In 2009, over 50% of registered studies failed to report race or ethnicity, or both; by 2024, this proportion had fallen to 17%; observational studies were consistently less likely than interventional trials to report race, ethnicity, or both</cite>. 
- Disease-specific trial cohorts: In adult acute leukemia trials (1998–2013), White patients had higher enrollment likelihood than Asian, Black/African American, or Hispanic participants (odds ratios 0.75, 0.48, and 0.44, respectively), illustrating underrepresentation that can reflect data collection/reporting biases and the need for subgroup-stratified analyses <cite id="4d23abfe-1">an evaluation of 15 cancer and leukemia Group B/alliance cooperative group adult acute leukemia clinical trials during 1998-2013 showed White patients had higher enrollment likelihood than their Asian, Black/African American, or Hispanic counterparts, with odds ratios of 0.75, 0.48, and 0.44 (all p < 0.01)</cite>. A recent hematologic malignancy phase III analysis reports that 76.3% of participants were White, with smaller proportions for Black/African American, American Indian/Alaska Native, Asian, and Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander, echoing long-standing disparities and data reporting limitations <cite id="4d23abfe-1">a substantial majority of participants in trials for hematological malignancies were White (76.3%), while smaller proportions were reported for Black/African American, American Indian/Alaska Native, Asian, and Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander</cite>. 
- Observational/real-world cohorts and registries: Cancer surveillance studies frequently face racial misclassification; a systematic review of 66 U.S. cancer surveillance articles found that 18% did not discuss or adjust for racial misclassification, while 83% did, but methods and categories varied widely; many comparisons focused on American Indian/Alaska Native versus non-Hispanic White populations, highlighting narrow framing and potential error in effect estimates <cite id="edc165f3-1">of the 66 articles on cancer surveillance among populations in the United States, 12 (18%) did not discuss racial misclassification or did not account for misclassification; 55 (83%) discussed misclassification, with 69% of articles comparing American Indian/Alaska Native with non-Hispanic White populations</cite>. Another review found that 10–16% of studies failed to address misclassification in methods, often using nontribal databases without adjustments; those that accounted for misclassification did so variably, underscoring pervasive underreporting and inconsistent handling <cite id="edc165f3-2">we found 11 (16%) studies that did not address racial misclassification; five (45%) of these used nontribal-based databases (e.g., National Center for Health Statistics, state cancer registries) without accounting for misclassification; four articles accounted for misclassification, but often noted it as a limitation without formal adjustment</cite>. In kidney transplantation, registry-based race classification differs from patient self-report, and misclassification likely biases surveillance and disparities estimates over time, especially for Asian, Hispanic/Latino, and Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander groups; authors recommend sensitivity analyses and expanded categories to mitigate bias <cite id="edc165f3-3">race classification was different across the 2 data sources for the same patients; misclassification has likely led to increasingly biased kidney transplantation research estimates over time, especially for populations classified as Asian, Hispanic/Latino, or Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander; improvements include acknowledging limitations, expanding categories, and including sensitivity analyses</cite>. 
- EHR-based cohorts and public health surveillance: EHR datasets often require harmonization and imputation to handle missing race/ethnicity; for example, researchers consolidated variables across systems using front-desk and portal self-identification, excluded participants with any missing anonymized covariates beyond race/ethnicity, and built a unified category to align with prior EHR research <cite id="e6f6e64c-3">self-reported race and ethnicity were collected at registration, kiosks, or via patient portals; a consolidated race and ethnicity variable was defined to harmonize definitions; individuals with missing data for any anonymized covariates besides race and ethnicity were excluded from analyses</cite>. In a COVID-19 testing cohort, 23% had unknown race/ethnicity, and 21.8% lacked race or 19.7% lacked ethnicity data, with missingness concentrated in younger adults and lower socioeconomic neighborhoods; imputing race/ethnicity changed subgroup composition and highlighted underrepresentation of males and individuals under 19, showing how missingness can distort epidemiologic inference <cite id="e6f6e64c-1">23.0% had an unknown race/ethnicity category; 21.8% missing race and 19.7% missing ethnicity; missing race/ethnicity was more likely in low-SVI tracts and younger or older adults; after imputing race/ethnicity, subgroup composition changed and males and those under 19 were underrepresented</cite>. When about one-third of records lack ethnicity, assumptions to fill gaps (e.g., defaulting to non-Hispanic) can attenuate or amplify observed disparities, and overlapping groupings complicate comparisons; CDC highlights that some data collection efforts still do not fully use OMB standards, further hampering accurate monitoring <cite id="e6f6e64c-4">with 35% missing ethnicity, assumptions that missing ethnicity implies non-Hispanic can distort disparity estimates; some data collection efforts still do not fully use OMB guidance for race/ethnicity, and alternative grouping methods yield different interpretations when data are incomplete</cite>. 
- Large cohorts and biobanks: The All of Us and UK Biobank cohorts rely on self-identification with country-specific categories that differ in structure and granularity (e.g., U.S. allows multiple groups; UK requires a single group with a “Mixed” option), and both are majority White; such sampling distributions can bias downstream modeling and downstream machine learning classification unless steps are taken to balance groups <cite id="e6f6e64c-2">All of Us and UKB participants self-identify race/ethnicity; the U.S. distinguishes race and ethnicity, while the UK defines ethnicity via national origins; All of Us is 54.0% White and UKB 94.4% White, leading to potential bias in machine learning; White participants were randomly down-sampled to balance group sizes</cite>. 
- Genomics and molecular profiling studies: Many genomic repositories suffer “missingness” of race/ethnicity, prompting researchers to impute self-reported categories from genetic ancestry to study disparities; for example, in colorectal cancer, race/ethnicity categories poorly capture shared ancestry in admixed groups, and investigators imputed race/ethnicity from genetic ancestry to address underreporting before evaluating molecular alterations, noting potential ascertainment biases in convenience samples <cite id="edc165f3-4">race and ethnicity categories may not capture shared ancestry well in highly admixed groups; genetic ancestry assessed via sequencing/genotyping can better capture ancestry; to address missingness of race/ethnicity common in this dataset, categories were imputed from genetic ancestry</cite>. 
- Policy-external cases: Even outside NIH-enforced settings, race/ethnicity reporting has been inadequate; for example, during COVID-19, a major trial of dexamethasone delayed reporting outcomes by race/ethnicity and another analysis collapsed all minorities into a single group, despite documented differences across non-white subgroups, illustrating how underreporting persists beyond mandate scope <cite id="4d23abfe-3">a trial investigating dexamethasone in COVID-19 delayed reporting outcomes by race/ethnicity; a hydroxychloroquine report grouped all racial/ethnic minorities into a singular population, despite evidence of group-specific differences</cite>.

Consequences for validity and fairness
- Bias and reduced generalizability: Persistent underreporting and misclassification of race/ethnicity can introduce information bias into surveillance reports and research, distort effect sizes, and reduce the generalizability of findings, particularly for underrepresented groups; disparities in enrollment likelihood and skewed denominators exacerbate these risks <cite id="4d23abfe-1">race misclassification in national, administrative data sources underestimates cancer cases by 16% to 37% for Asians and distorts disparities; White patients had higher enrollment likelihood than Asian, Black/African American, and Hispanic participants</cite> <cite id="edc165f3-3">misclassification of race in kidney transplantation data has likely introduced information bias into surveillance and research, especially for Asian, Hispanic/Latino, and Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander populations</cite>. 
- Analytical uncertainty and policy risk: When missingness is high or handled with naive assumptions, disparity estimates can be attenuated or amplified, leading to different conclusions and potentially misguided interventions; experts therefore recommend explicit misclassification-aware methods, expanded categories, and sensitivity analyses when race/ethnicity data are incomplete <cite id="e6f6e64c-4">assumptions when ethnicity is missing can attenuate or amplify disparities; alternative methods for grouping race/ethnicity when data are incomplete can lead to different interpretations and highlight the need for expert methods</cite> <cite id="edc165f3-3">expanding race/ethnicity categories and including sensitivity analyses accounting for misclassification are recommended to mitigate information bias</cite>.

Mitigations and ways forward
- Strengthen audit and enforcement: Align trial and surveillance reporting with registry mandates and apply consistent penalties and support for compliance; observational studies need targeted guidance and resources to report sociodemographics routinely <cite id="4d23abfe-0">Previous analyses have shown that trials delay reporting results to ClinicalTrials.gov, despite ethical and regulatory mandates; observational studies were consistently less likely than interventional trials to report race/ethnicity</cite>. 
- Harmonize and standardize categories: Use OMB standards and allow multiple-group selection where meaningful, expand categories (e.g., skin tone, ancestry), and avoid collapsing multiple minority groups; provide harmonization guidance for cross-dataset analyses <cite id="e6f6e64c-4">some data collection efforts still do not fully use OMB standards for race/ethnicity; alternative grouping methods and imputation can improve estimates when data are incomplete</cite> <cite id="e6f6e64c-2">the U.S. allows multiple groups while the UK requires a single group with a “Mixed” category, creating cross-system challenges that require careful harmonization</cite>. 
- Improve data quality and transparency: Collect race/ethnicity at point-of-care and registration consistently, retain multiple modalities (self-report, provider report), and document missingness; perform imputation with explicit assumptions and publish sensitivity analyses to misclassification and subgroup incompleteness <cite id="e6f6e64c-3">race/ethnicity were collected at registration, kiosks, or portals with multiple entries; a consolidated variable was defined to align with prior research</cite> <cite id="edc165f3-3">improvements include acknowledging limitations, expanding categories, including sensitivity analyses accounting for race misclassification, supplementing with interviews, and including write-in options</cite>. 
- Use biological anchors where appropriate: In admixed or genomic studies, supplement self-reported categories with genetic ancestry inference to reduce misclassification and address missingness, while recognizing ancestry–environment interactions and reporting limitations <cite id="edc165f3-4">genetic ancestry can better capture ancestry than self-reported categories in admixed groups; race/ethnicity were imputed from genetic ancestry to address missingness, with caveats about ascertainment bias</cite>.

Summary
Across clinical trials, observational cohorts, registries, and public health surveillance, race/ethnicity are frequently underreported, inconsistently categorized, or incompletely analyzed despite longstanding mandates. Documented patterns include large fractions of studies omitting race/ethnicity, skewed category distributions misaligned with Census benchmarks, high missingness in EHR and testing datasets, and frequent misclassification in administrative and registry systems—all of which can bias effect estimates and obscure subgroup-specific effects. Concrete mitigation strategies include stronger audit/oversight, category harmonization aligned with OMB standards, transparent handling of missingness, and, where appropriate, integration of genetic ancestry with clear caveats about interpretation. <cite id="4d23abfe-0">In 2009, over 50% of registered studies failed to report race or ethnicity, with observational studies consistently less likely to report than interventional trials</cite> <cite id="4d23abfe-4">in 2024, 17.2% of studies still did not report any race/ethnicity and 28.2% reported only one of the two; category distributions skewed toward “White” and “Not Hispanic or Latino” and did not align with Census data</cite> <cite id="4d23abfe-1">76.3% White participants in hematologic malignancy trials and odds ratios indicating lower enrollment likelihood for Asian, Black/African American, and Hispanic participants</cite> <cite id="edc165f3-1">18% of cancer surveillance articles did not address racial misclassification, with 83% discussing it variably</cite> <cite id="e6f6e64c-1">23.0% unknown race/ethnicity and 21.8% missing race (19.7% missing ethnicity) in a COVID-19 testing cohort, with imputation revealing subgroup underrepresentation and demographic skews</cite> <cite id="e6f6e64c-2">All of Us and UK Biobank self-identification categories differ and both are majority White, requiring careful harmonization and sometimes down-sampling to avoid bias</cite> <cite id="edc165f3-4">genomic datasets often face missingness common enough to impute from genetic ancestry, but convenience sampling and category limitations persist</cite> <cite id="4d23abfe-3">major COVID-19 reports delayed or collapsed race/ethnicity reporting, underscoring persistence of underreporting even outside NIH mandates</cite>.

Title: The Urgency of Justice in Research: Beyond COVID-19
Snippet: Research participation inequities persist despite over 25 years of mandated inclusion and reporting policies from the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the world's largest public funder of biomedical research [6,7] (Box 1). Major research reports often omit or delay reporting demographics and outcomes by subpopulation [7], contravening NIH requirements viii,ix . Similar omissions are observed globally and among studies not subject to NIH policies, such as a trial investigating the efficacy of dexamethasone in reducing mortality among hospitalized patients with COVID-19, which delayed reporting outcomes by race/ethnicity [8]. In a separate report evaluating hydroxychloroquine, all racial/ethnic minorities were grouped into a singular population [9], despite evidence indicating group-specific differences in outcomes across non-white demographics i [10]. This illustrates the need for both improved engagement and inclusion, as well as broader adoption of transparent reporting and accountability structures, encompassing both appropriate detail and effective enforcement. Inequities often intersect, particularly across geographic and socioeconomic strata, yet measures of inclusivity often overlook socioeconomically disadvantaged or otherwise marginalized populations, such as disabled, unhoused, rural, older, institutionalized, hearing and vision impaired, justice system-involved persons, and sexual and gender minorities, each of which face distinct barriers to research accessibility. We must routinely measure and intervene upon intersecting, overlapping, and interacting dimensions of vulnerability to exclusion. Funding agencies, editors, reviewers, institutional review boards, and researchers all bear this responsibility.

Promoting accountability necessitates a shift away from assuming prospective participants as distrustful to assuming researchers and institutions must demonstrate trustworthiness. Title: Investigation of Treatment‐Related Disparities in Metastatic Pancreatic Cancer Patients Using Real‐World Data
Snippet: The patients are ascertained from private practice oncology clinics and tertiary care centers; patients seen at safety-net hospitals are not included in this dataset. Further, as in any observational study, there may be biases due to unmeasured confounding. Factors such as income, marital status, and comorbidity score are not available for analysis, and omission of such variables could bias findings. Data are also subject to misclassification or missingness; although we used multiple imputation methods to deal with missing data in our analysis, this relies on the assumption that the data are missing at random. Finally, it is important to note that the race and ethnicity data used in this study were selfreported, reflecting individuals' social identities rather than genetic ancestry. Self-reported race is influenced by sociopolitical and cultural factors, which shape healthcare access, provider biases, and treatment decisions [29]. This distinction is critical, as race is a social construct that does not correspond to underlying genetic differences but rather to lived experiences and systemic inequities [29]. In contrast, genetic ancestry reflects inherited genetic variation and does not inherently drive disparities in healthcare outcomes. Understanding these distinctions is essential for interpreting racial disparities in medical research and underscores the need for policies that address the structural and societal factors contributing to inequities in cancer treatment and outcomes.
</snippet>

The race and ethnic groups are similar for both countries, albeit with differences that reflect the distinct patterns of immigration and resulting demographic characteristics of each country. Below are concrete, documented examples of underreporting and poor standardization of race/ethnicity in research despite existing mandates, along with analyses of why it persists and what the consequences are.

Why underreporting persists despite mandates
- Policy coverage and heterogeneity: Multiple U.S. policies since the 1990s require collection and reporting of race/ethnicity for NIH-funded studies, FDA-regulated trials, and public health surveillance, yet compliance and enforcement remain inconsistent across sponsors, institutions, and countries, with variations in definitions and collection procedures contributing to incomplete or nonstandardized data <cite id="4d23abfe-1">Various policies and guidelines have been issued regarding the reporting of race and ethnicity data for the U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH)-funded trial participants since the 1990s; in 2016, the NIH introduced a final rule mandating that demographic characteristics, including race and ethnicity, be reported in ClinicalTrials.gov; despite these policies and guidelines, reporting remains insufficient with inconsistent enforcement and compliance, with variations in race/ethnicity definitions and collection across studies</cite>. 
- Sponsor/institutional capacity and incentives: Sponsors and research teams may lack accountability resources or face misalignment of incentives, and data security/privacy concerns can deter disclosure of sensitive identity attributes like race/ethnicity, further reducing reporting; observational studies are less likely than interventional trials to report race/ethnicity even when data are available <cite id="4d23abfe-1">some sponsors and researchers may lack accountability or resources to adhere strictly to reporting standards; trial participants may be reluctant to disclose sensitive personal information, including race and ethnicity data, given data security and privacy concerns</cite> <cite id="4d23abfe-0">Across all study years, observational studies were consistently less likely than interventional trials to report race, ethnicity, or both</cite>.
- Cross-national variation and language resources: International trials face multilingual and cross-country differences in racial/ethnic classification, contributing to underreporting and misalignment with U.S. standards; these issues are visible in the underrepresentation of Asian groups in global trials registered in ClinicalTrials.gov despite their prevalence in the U.S. and worldwide <cite id="4d23abfe-0">the availability of multilingual recruitment and reporting resources is critical to diversity initiatives; the low and declining percentage of Asian and other racial groups is concerning, especially considering the large prevalence of Asian individuals in the US and globally</cite>.
- Enforcement gaps and delayed/omitted subgroup analyses: Even when policies exist, major reports have omitted or delayed reporting of outcomes by race/ethnicity and collapsed multiple minority groups into a single category, undermining the intent of mandates and masking group-specific effects, as seen in COVID-19 analyses <cite id="4d23abfe-3">Major research reports often omit or delay reporting demographics and outcomes by subpopulation, contravening NIH requirements; a trial investigating dexamethasone delayed reporting outcomes by race/ethnicity; in a separate report evaluating hydroxychloroquine, all racial/ethnic minorities were grouped into a singular population, despite evidence of group-specific differences</cite>.

Concrete examples and magnitudes across study types
- Clinical trials and trial registries: A 2009–2024 analysis of ClinicalTrials.gov shows that while reporting has improved, in 2024 about one in five studies still provided no race/ethnicity data (17.2%) and nearly one-third reported only race or only ethnicity (28.2%); categories were skewed toward “White” and “Not Hispanic or Latino,” and did not align with Census distributions, indicating both underreporting and misclassification risks <cite id="4d23abfe-4">In 2024, 17.2% of studies still did not report any data on race and ethnicity, and 28.2% only reported either race or ethnicity; “Not Hispanic or Latino” and “White” were the most common categories across time, with the breakdown of race and ethnicity categories not aligning with Census data across time</cite>. Earlier, more than half of registered studies had failed to report race/ethnicity by the late 2000s, and observational studies were persistently less likely than interventional trials to report these demographics <cite id="4d23abfe-0">In 2009, over 50% of registered studies failed to report race or ethnicity, or both; by 2024, this proportion had fallen to 17%; observational studies were consistently less likely than interventional trials to report race, ethnicity, or both</cite>. 
- Disease-specific trial cohorts: In adult acute leukemia trials (1998–2013), White patients had higher enrollment likelihood than Asian, Black/African American, or Hispanic participants (odds ratios 0.75, 0.48, and 0.44, respectively), illustrating underrepresentation that can reflect data collection/reporting biases and the need for subgroup-stratified analyses <cite id="4d23abfe-1">an evaluation of 15 cancer and leukemia Group B/alliance cooperative group adult acute leukemia clinical trials during 1998-2013 showed White patients had higher enrollment likelihood than their Asian, Black/African American, or Hispanic counterparts, with odds ratios of 0.75, 0.48, and 0.44 (all p < 0.01)</cite>. A recent hematologic malignancy phase III analysis reports that 76.3% of participants were White, with smaller proportions for Black/African American, American Indian/Alaska Native, Asian, and Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander, echoing long-standing disparities and data reporting limitations <cite id="4d23abfe-1">a substantial majority of participants in trials for hematological malignancies were White (76.3%), while smaller proportions were reported for Black/African American, American Indian/Alaska Native, Asian, and Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander</cite>. 
- Observational/real-world cohorts and registries: Cancer surveillance studies frequently face racial misclassification; a systematic review of 66 U.S. cancer surveillance articles found that 18% did not discuss or adjust for racial misclassification, while 83% did, but methods and categories varied widely; many comparisons focused on American Indian/Alaska Native versus non-Hispanic White populations, highlighting narrow framing and potential error in effect estimates <cite id="edc165f3-1">of the 66 articles on cancer surveillance among populations in the United States, 12 (18%) did not discuss racial misclassification or did not account for misclassification; 55 (83%) discussed misclassification, with 69% of articles comparing American Indian/Alaska Native with non-Hispanic White populations</cite>. Another review found that 10–16% of studies failed to address misclassification in methods, often using nontribal databases without adjustments; those that accounted for misclassification did so variably, underscoring pervasive underreporting and inconsistent handling <cite id="edc165f3-2">we found 11 (16%) studies that did not address racial misclassification; five (45%) of these used nontribal-based databases (e.g., National Center for Health Statistics, state cancer registries) without accounting for misclassification; four articles accounted for misclassification, but often noted it as a limitation without formal adjustment</cite>. In kidney transplantation, registry-based race classification differs from patient self-report, and misclassification likely biases surveillance and disparities estimates over time, especially for Asian, Hispanic/Latino, and Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander groups; authors recommend sensitivity analyses and expanded categories to mitigate bias <cite id="edc165f3-3">race classification was different across the 2 data sources for the same patients; misclassification has likely led to increasingly biased kidney transplantation research estimates over time, especially for populations classified as Asian, Hispanic/Latino, or Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander; improvements include acknowledging limitations, expanding categories, and including sensitivity analyses</cite>. 
- EHR-based cohorts and public health surveillance: EHR datasets often require harmonization and imputation to handle missing race/ethnicity; for example, researchers consolidated variables across systems using front-desk and portal self-identification, excluded participants with any missing anonymized covariates beyond race/ethnicity, and built a unified category to align with prior EHR research <cite id="e6f6e64c-3">self-reported race and ethnicity were collected at registration, kiosks, or via patient portals; a consolidated race and ethnicity variable was defined to harmonize definitions; individuals with missing data for any anonymized covariates besides race and ethnicity were excluded from analyses</cite>. In a COVID-19 testing cohort, 23% had unknown race/ethnicity, and 21.8% lacked race or 19.7% lacked ethnicity data, with missingness concentrated in younger adults and lower socioeconomic neighborhoods; imputing race/ethnicity changed subgroup composition and highlighted underrepresentation of males and individuals under 19, showing how missingness can distort epidemiologic inference <cite id="e6f6e64c-1">23.0% had an unknown race/ethnicity category; 21.8% missing race and 19.7% missing ethnicity; missing race/ethnicity was more likely in low-SVI tracts and younger or older adults; after imputing race/ethnicity, subgroup composition changed and males and those under 19 were underrepresented</cite>. When about one-third of records lack ethnicity, assumptions to fill gaps (e.g., defaulting to non-Hispanic) can attenuate or amplify observed disparities, and overlapping groupings complicate comparisons; CDC highlights that some data collection efforts still do not fully use OMB standards, further hampering accurate monitoring <cite id="e6f6e64c-4">with 35% missing ethnicity, assumptions that missing ethnicity implies non-Hispanic can distort disparity estimates; some data collection efforts still do not fully use OMB guidance for race/ethnicity, and alternative grouping methods yield different interpretations when data are incomplete</cite>. 
- Large cohorts and biobanks: The All of Us and UK Biobank cohorts rely on self-identification with country-specific categories that differ in structure and granularity (e.g., U.S. allows multiple groups; UK requires a single group with a “Mixed” option), and both are majority White; such sampling distributions can bias downstream modeling and downstream machine learning classification unless steps are taken to balance groups <cite id="e6f6e64c-2">All of Us and UKB participants self-identify race/ethnicity; the U.S. distinguishes race and ethnicity, while the UK defines ethnicity via national origins; All of Us is 54.0% White and UKB 94.4% White, leading to potential bias in machine learning; White participants were randomly down-sampled to balance group sizes</cite>. 
- Genomics and molecular profiling studies: Many genomic repositories suffer “missingness” of race/ethnicity, prompting researchers to impute self-reported categories from genetic ancestry to study disparities; for example, in colorectal cancer, race/ethnicity categories poorly capture shared ancestry in admixed groups, and investigators imputed race/ethnicity from genetic ancestry to address underreporting before evaluating molecular alterations, noting potential ascertainment biases in convenience samples <cite id="edc165f3-4">race and ethnicity categories may not capture shared ancestry well in highly admixed groups; genetic ancestry assessed via sequencing/genotyping can better capture ancestry; to address missingness of race/ethnicity common in this dataset, categories were imputed from genetic ancestry</cite>. 
- Policy-external cases: Even outside NIH-enforced settings, race/ethnicity reporting has been inadequate; for example, during COVID-19, a major trial of dexamethasone delayed reporting outcomes by race/ethnicity and another analysis collapsed all minorities into a single group, despite documented differences across non-white subgroups, illustrating how underreporting persists beyond mandate scope <cite id="4d23abfe-3">a trial investigating dexamethasone in COVID-19 delayed reporting outcomes by race/ethnicity; a hydroxychloroquine report grouped all racial/ethnic minorities into a singular population, despite evidence of group-specific differences</cite>.

Consequences for validity and fairness
- Bias and reduced generalizability: Persistent underreporting and misclassification of race/ethnicity can introduce information bias into surveillance reports and research, distort effect sizes, and reduce the generalizability of findings, particularly for underrepresented groups; disparities in enrollment likelihood and skewed denominators exacerbate these risks <cite id="4d23abfe-1">race misclassification in national, administrative data sources underestimates cancer cases by 16% to 37% for Asians and distorts disparities; White patients had higher enrollment likelihood than Asian, Black/African American, and Hispanic participants</cite> <cite id="edc165f3-3">misclassification of race in kidney transplantation data has likely introduced information bias into surveillance and research, especially for Asian, Hispanic/Latino, and Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander populations</cite>. 
- Analytical uncertainty and policy risk: When missingness is high or handled with naive assumptions, disparity estimates can be attenuated or amplified, leading to different conclusions and potentially misguided interventions; experts therefore recommend explicit misclassification-aware methods, expanded categories, and sensitivity analyses when race/ethnicity data are incomplete <cite id="e6f6e64c-4">assumptions when ethnicity is missing can attenuate or amplify disparities; alternative methods for grouping race/ethnicity when data are incomplete can lead to different interpretations and highlight the need for expert methods</cite> <cite id="edc165f3-3">expanding race/ethnicity categories and including sensitivity analyses accounting for misclassification are recommended to mitigate information bias</cite>.

Mitigations and ways forward
- Strengthen audit and enforcement: Align trial and surveillance reporting with registry mandates and apply consistent penalties and support for compliance; observational studies need targeted guidance and resources to report sociodemographics routinely <cite id="4d23abfe-0">Previous analyses have shown that trials delay reporting results to ClinicalTrials.gov, despite ethical and regulatory mandates; observational studies were consistently less likely than interventional trials to report race/ethnicity</cite>. 
- Harmonize and standardize categories: Use OMB standards and allow multiple-group selection where meaningful, expand categories (e.g., skin tone, ancestry), and avoid collapsing multiple minority groups; provide harmonization guidance for cross-dataset analyses <cite id="e6f6e64c-4">some data collection efforts still do not fully use OMB standards for race/ethnicity; alternative grouping methods and imputation can improve estimates when data are incomplete</cite> <cite id="e6f6e64c-2">the U.S. allows multiple groups while the UK requires a single group with a “Mixed” category, creating cross-system challenges that require careful harmonization</cite>. 
- Improve data quality and transparency: Collect race/ethnicity at point-of-care and registration consistently, retain multiple modalities (self-report, provider report), and document missingness; perform imputation with explicit assumptions and publish sensitivity analyses to misclassification and subgroup incompleteness <cite id="e6f6e64c-3">race/ethnicity were collected at registration, kiosks, or portals with multiple entries; a consolidated variable was defined to align with prior research</cite> <cite id="edc165f3-3">improvements include acknowledging limitations, expanding categories, including sensitivity analyses accounting for race misclassification, supplementing with interviews, and including write-in options</cite>. 
- Use biological anchors where appropriate: In admixed or genomic studies, supplement self-reported categories with genetic ancestry inference to reduce misclassification and address missingness, while recognizing ancestry–environment interactions and reporting limitations <cite id="edc165f3-4">genetic ancestry can better capture ancestry than self-reported categories in admixed groups; race/ethnicity were imputed from genetic ancestry to address missingness, with caveats about ascertainment bias</cite>.

Summary
Across clinical trials, observational cohorts, registries, and public health surveillance, race/ethnicity are frequently underreported, inconsistently categorized, or incompletely analyzed despite longstanding mandates. Documented patterns include large fractions of studies omitting race/ethnicity, skewed category distributions misaligned with Census benchmarks, high missingness in EHR and testing datasets, and frequent misclassification in administrative and registry systems—all of which can bias effect estimates and obscure subgroup-specific effects. Concrete mitigation strategies include stronger audit/oversight, category harmonization aligned with OMB standards, transparent handling of missingness, and, where appropriate, integration of genetic ancestry with clear caveats about interpretation. <cite id="4d23abfe-0">In 2009, over 50% of registered studies failed to report race or ethnicity, with observational studies consistently less likely to report than interventional trials</cite> <cite id="4d23abfe-4">in 2024, 17.2% of studies still did not report any race/ethnicity and 28.2% reported only one of the two; category distributions skewed toward “White” and “Not Hispanic or Latino” and did not align with Census data</cite> <cite id="4d23abfe-1">76.3% White participants in hematologic malignancy trials and odds ratios indicating lower enrollment likelihood for Asian, Black/African American, and Hispanic participants</cite> <cite id="edc165f3-1">18% of cancer surveillance articles did not address racial misclassification, with 83% discussing it variably</cite> <cite id="e6f6e64c-1">23.0% unknown race/ethnicity and 21.8% missing race (19.7% missing ethnicity) in a COVID-19 testing cohort, with imputation revealing subgroup underrepresentation and demographic skews</cite> <cite id="e6f6e64c-2">All of Us and UK Biobank self-identification categories differ and both are majority White, requiring careful harmonization and sometimes down-sampling to avoid bias</cite> <cite id="edc165f3-4">genomic datasets often face missingness common enough to impute from genetic ancestry, but convenience sampling and category limitations persist</cite> <cite id="4d23abfe-3">major COVID-19 reports delayed or collapsed race/ethnicity reporting, underscoring persistence of underreporting even outside NIH mandates</cite>.</answer>

Title: Racial and Ethnic Diversity in Clinical Studies Reported to ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009–2024
Snippet: To our knowledge, this is the first study to systematically document long-term trends in the reporting of race and ethnicity to clinicaltrials.gov and to quantify the characteristics of studies that are more likely to report race and ethnicity. Sufficient representation in clinical studies are essential in evaluating interventions and products across diverse populations, ensuring that they do not reinforce existing biases. In 2009, over 50% of registered studies failed to report race or ethnicity, or both; by 2024, this proportion had fallen to 17%. Early-phase trials, interventional trials, and studies that are conducted in the US were most likely to report race and ethnicity. Among US studies, the frequency of race and ethnicity reporting between federally sponsored and industry sponsored studies. However, NIH-funded studies were more likely to report both race and ethnicity. 

Race is more commonly reported than ethnicity; however, in recent years over half of registered studies report both race and ethnicity, and more than three-quarters report race alone. In 2024, most adult participants were classified as either White or Black. Given that clinicaltrials.gov also includes international studies, the low and declining percentage of Asian . and other racial groups is concerning, especially considering the large prevalence of Asian individuals in the US and globally. While the geographic context and racial dynamics of the countries where the research is being conducted must be considered, the availability of multilingual recruitment and reporting resources is critical to diversity initiatives. 29 Across all study years, observational studies were consistently less likely than interventional trials to report race, ethnicity, or both. Title: Investigation of Treatment‐Related Disparities in Metastatic Pancreatic Cancer Patients Using Real‐World Data
Snippet: The patients are ascertained from private practice oncology clinics and tertiary care centers; patients seen at safety-net hospitals are not included in this dataset. Further, as in any observational study, there may be biases due to unmeasured confounding. Factors such as income, marital status, and comorbidity score are not available for analysis, and omission of such variables could bias findings. Data are also subject to misclassification or missingness; although we used multiple imputation methods to deal with missing data in our analysis, this relies on the assumption that the data are missing at random. Finally, it is important to note that the race and ethnicity data used in this study were selfreported, reflecting individuals' social identities rather than genetic ancestry. Self-reported race is influenced by sociopolitical and cultural factors, which shape healthcare access, provider biases, and treatment decisions [29]. This distinction is critical, as race is a social construct that does not correspond to underlying genetic differences but rather to lived experiences and systemic inequities [29]. In contrast, genetic ancestry reflects inherited genetic variation and does not inherently drive disparities in healthcare outcomes. Understanding these distinctions is essential for interpreting racial disparities in medical research and underscores the need for policies that address the structural and societal factors contributing to inequities in cancer treatment and outcomes.

Title: Association of genetic ancestry with molecular tumor profiles in colorectal cancer
Snippet: Furthermore, race and ethnicity categories may not capture shared ancestry well in highly admixed groups such as Black and Hispanic/Latino patients [16]. In contrast, genetic ancestry, assessed via a patient's sequencing or genotyping data, can potentially better capture genotypic profiles associated with risk, though it is important to understand that genetic ancestry is also associated with environmental risks [17].

Title: Missing data and missed infections: investigating racial and ethnic disparities in SARS-CoV-2 testing and infection rates in Holyoke, Massachusetts
Snippet: In the Holyoke testing population, 23.0% of individuals had an unknown race and ethnicity category (n = 4 531), with 21.8% (n = 4 286) missing data on race, 19.7% (n = 3 869) missing data on ethnicity, and less than 1% missing data on age (n = 14) (Table 1).Individuals with missing race and/or ethnicity data were more likely to reside in low-SVI census tracts, be under the age of 45 years or over age 84 years, have a lower total number of PCR tests, have an earlier week of first test, and live in a house versus an apartment.These individuals were less likely to have had an antibody test or to have ever tested positive (Table S2).

After imputing race and ethnicity, the size of the non-Hispanic Asian population in the imputed testing data was slightly larger than the Holyoke population, leading to a significantly larger proportion of non-Hispanic Asian individuals in the imputed testing data.Further, we found significant but not meaningful differences (all <1%) in all racial and ethnic categories between individuals who received at least 1 test and the Holyoke population.The distribution of SVIs was similar between the Holyoke population and the imputed testing data.Individuals under age 19 years and males were underrepresented in the imputed testing data in comparison with the city population, while individuals aged 20-44 years were overrepresented.

Title: Race, Ethnicity, and Pharmacogenomic Variation in the United States and the United Kingdom
Snippet: All of Us and UKB volunteer participants self-identify their race and ethnicity upon enrollment. All of Us race and ethnic groups are defined based on the US Census standards, and UKB ethnic groups are defined based on the UK National Health Service (NHS) standards. The US makes a distinction between race based on ancestral origins, and ethnicity based on shared culture, whereas the UK defines ethnicity based on shared national origins. The race and ethnic groups are similar for both countries, albeit with differences that reflect the distinct patterns of immigration and resulting demographic characteristics of each country. For example, the Hispanic ethnic category exists only in the US, and the Asian category in the UK covers South Asian immigrants from Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan, with Chinese broken out as a separate group. The US classification allows for the selection of More than one group, whereas the UK classification requires the selection of a single ethnic group but includes a Mixed category. 

The All of Us participant cohort is 54.0% White, 19.6% Black or African American, 15.9% Hispanic or Latino, 3.1% Asian, and 3.6% More than one; the UKB participant cohort is 94.4% White, 1.9% Asian, 1.5% Black, 0.3% Chinese, and 0.6% Mixed. Although the All of Us cohort is substantially more racially/ethnically diverse than UKB, White participants make up the majority of each biobank, which could bias machine learning classification algorithms. Accordingly, White participants were randomly down-sampled to 20,000 participants for All of Us and 10,000 participants for UKB to yield more balanced group sample sizes for subsequent machine learning prediction (Table 1). Both biobanks have more female than male participants; the All of Us cohort is 60.8% female and UKB is 53.4% female. The average age for both biobanks is 53 years.

Snippet: A consolidated race and ethnicity variable was defined to harmonize definitions across NYU and INSIGHT and to align with prior EHR-based research [23]. Within NYU, self-reported race and ethnicity was defined using distinct race and ethnicity fields in the Epic Clarity database. Race and ethnicity are collected at front desk registration, at self-check-in kiosks, or through patient portals (i.e., MyChart). These fields allow for multiple entries of racial or ethnic categories. The consolidated race and ethnicity variable was defined using the following hierarchy: 

(1) Latino-any Hispanic/Latino/Spanish race or ethnicity; (  [24]. Title: Alternative Methods for Grouping Race and Ethnicity to Monitor COVID-19 Outcomes and Vaccination Coverage
Snippet: The denominators for rate calculations are either persons reported as Hispanic or persons reported as a race category and non-Hispanic, with an assumption in method A that persons for whom missing ethnicity data were missing are non-Hispanic. Method A is more commonly used when ethnicity is missing from a small percentage of records and other information in the record supports a non-Hispanic designation. When approximately one-third of records are missing ethnicity, as in this report (35% for case and 32% for vaccination coverage data), that assumption might attenuate or amplify disparities for certain groups. With method B, the race and ethnicity groups are not mutually exclusive. This complicates comparisons that use a reference group (often White persons), because the race and ethnicity categories overlap. The findings in this report are subject to at least four limitations. First, because the analysis did not include persons who identified as multiple races or other race, conclusions cannot be drawn about the use of the alternative methods for grouping and analyzing these racial categories. Second, this report did not explore all possible analytic methods for grouping race and ethnicity. For example, imputation (i.e., replacing missing data with other values) has been examined as a potential method to improve estimates of COVID-19 racial and ethnic disparities (6). Third, data shared with CDC might undercount COVID-19 cases and vaccination coverage and this undercount might differ by race or ethnicity. Finally, although progress has been made to incorporate the Office of Management and Budget standards (such as Statistical Policy Directive No. 15) into the collection and presentation of race and ethnicity data, some data collection efforts still do not fully use this guidance (7). 

Although race and ethnicity are not the only measures for assessing health disparities, these measures have been integral to CDC's understanding of the health outcomes associated with COVID-19 (8)(9)(10). This analysis demonstrates that alternative methods for analyzing race and ethnicity data when data are incomplete can lead to different interpretations about disparities and highlights the importance of working with experts to identify methods for analyzing and tracking disparities when race and ethnicity data are incomplete.

documents.title: Race, Ethnicity, and Pharmacogenomic Variation in the United States and the United Kingdom
documents.snippet:
All of Us and UKB volunteer participants self-identify their race and ethnicity upon enrollment. All of Us race and ethnic groups are defined based on the US Census standards, and UKB ethnic groups are defined based on the UK National Health Service (NHS) standards. The US makes a distinction between race based on ancestral origins, and ethnicity based on shared culture, whereas the UK defines ethnicity based on shared national origins. The race and ethnic groups are similar for both countries, albeit with differences that reflect the distinct patterns of immigration and resulting demographic characteristics of each country. For example, the Hispanic ethnic category exists only in the US, and the Asian category in the UK covers South Asian immigrants from Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan, with Chinese broken out as a separate group. The US classification allows for the selection of More than one group, whereas the UK classification requires the selection of a single ethnic group but includes a Mixed category. 

The All of Us participant cohort is 54.0% White, 19.6% Black or African American, 15.9% Hispanic or Latino, 3.1% Asian, and 3.6% More than one; the UKB participant cohort is 94.4% White, 1.9% Asian, 1.5% Black, 0.3% Chinese, and 0.6% Mixed. Although the All of Us cohort is substantially more racially/ethnically diverse than UKB, White participants make up the majority of each biobank, which could bias machine learning classification algorithms. Accordingly, White participants were randomly down-sampled to 20,000 participants for All of Us and 10,000 participants for UKB to yield more balanced group sample sizes for subsequent machine learning prediction (Table 1). Both biobanks have more female than male participants; the All of Us cohort is 60.8% female and UKB is 53.4% female. The average age for both biobanks is 53 years.

attempts.answer:
Summary
Despite overlapping federal mandates, NIH-funded studies and industry-sponsored trials differ in their incentives, governance, and operational context for collecting and reporting race/ethnicity, which helps explain the lower reporting and representation in industry trials. <cite id="fb1656b1-1">Across two decades of >20,000 US-based trials, industry-funded studies were associated with less race/ethnicity reporting and lower minority enrollment than US government-funded trials, even after controlling for other features</cite>. <cite id="fb1656b1-0">Within tumor therapies, NIH-funded studies were the most consistent reporters of race and ethnicity, while industry-funded trials showed an upward trend in race reporting but not ethnicity reporting</cite>. These differences are not due to the absence of mandates: <cite id="359bcb79-2">federal initiatives since the 1990s, including OMB standards and FDA guidance, standardize race/ethnicity categories and expect sponsors to collect and report such data for regulatory applications</cite>, and <cite id="fbf58093-1">NIH policy since 2017 requires NIH-funded studies to report race/ethnicity on ClinicalTrials.gov</cite>. Below, we synthesize why compliance and completeness still diverge.

What the mandates require and how they apply differently
- NIH/Common Rule and FDA set the baseline requirements. <cite id="359bcb79-2">The NIH Revitalization Act (1993), FDA guidance (1999 and 2005), and OMB standards collectively require standardized collection and reporting of race/ethnicity in biomedical research and drug development</cite>, providing the common categories (race: American Indian/Alaska Native, Asian, Black or African American, Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander, White; ethnicity: Hispanic/Latino vs. Not Hispanic/Latino). <cite id="fbf58093-0">NIH’s 2016 final rule for clinical trial registration and results reporting mandates demographic characteristics—including race and ethnicity—on ClinicalTrials.gov</cite>. <cite id="359bcb79-3">FDA’s guidance emphasizes enhanced diversity and standardization of race/ethnicity data collection for trials that support labeling and approvals</cite>.
- Despite identical “identical” mandates, scope and enforcement differ by setting. <cite id="359bcb79-0">An NIH-funded investigator-initiated study must meet NIH policy, the Common Rule, and applicable FDA regulations; FDA has proposed—and may implement—an investigator/IDE-exempt sIRB rule that would differ from both NIH and the Common Rule, creating practical ambiguity in how policies interplay</cite>. <cite id="359bcb79-0">NIH and OHRP exceptions to single-IRB reliance do not fully align, and multiple regulatory bodies may co-oversight, complicating compliance pathways</cite>. These administrative frictions can slow or dilute implementation in complex, multi-sponsor contexts that are common in industry consortia.

Empirical differences in reporting and representation
- Industry vs. NIH: <cite id="fb1656b1-1">A cohort study of 20,000+ trials found fewer than 44% reported any race/ethnicity data overall, and industry-funded trials had lower race/ethnicity reporting and lower minority enrollment than government-funded trials, even after conditioning on other trial features</cite>. <cite id="fb1656b1-3">Analyses of enrollment also suggest industry sponsorship is associated with greater White enrollment, potentially reflecting regulatory and financial incentives that reduce perceived confounding from patient-related factors, while showing smaller but positive trends for Latino enrollment relative to government-funded trials</cite>. <cite id="fb1656b1-0">In glioma therapy trials, NIH-funded studies were the most consistent in reporting both race and ethnicity; industry-sponsored trials improved over time for race but not ethnicity</cite>.
- NIH studies still have gaps: <cite id="fb1656b1-2">In pediatric NIH-funded trials, reporting of race/ethnicity remains incomplete across publications and ClinicalTrials.gov</cite>, indicating that mandates alone do not guarantee universal capture.

Organizational and incentive-based reasons specific to industry trials
- Sponsor control and financial incentives: <cite id="fb1656b1-3">Industry sponsorship is associated with enrollment patterns that may reflect regulatory and financial incentives favoring homogeneity to reduce risk of confounding, which can indirectly discourage detailed demographic reporting and recruitment of heterogeneous groups</cite>. <cite id="fbf58093-2">FDA reviewers often find subgroup analyses limited by small samples and treated as secondary/exploratory, which may disincentivize sponsors from investing resources in detailed race/ethnicity stratification unless a regulator flags race/ethnicity as a risk management concern (e.g., via a Race/Ethnicity Pre-Approval Requirement/Caveat, PMR/C)</cite>. <cite id="fb1656b1-3">Only a minority of trials received such PMR/Cs, suggesting limited regulatory leverage to enforce robust subgroup reporting in routine approvals</cite>.
- Publication norms and pressure to publish efficacy: <cite id="fb1656b1-1">Industry-funded trials tend to be less likely to report race/ethnicity demographics than government-funded trials, and smaller trials are less likely to report race/ethnicity at all</cite>. In industry portfolios, emphasis may be placed on time-to-approval and headline efficacy rather than demographic breakdowns that are ancillary to peer review or investor audiences, reducing perceived value and priority for comprehensive demographic capture. <cite id="fbf58093-0">Sponsors and researchers may lack accountability or resources to adhere strictly to reporting standards, and privacy concerns can impede participant willingness to disclose race/ethnicity</cite>.
- Trial design and scale: <cite id="fb1656b1-1">Smaller trials are less likely to report race/ethnicity demographics; industry sponsors run many smaller, global, or early-phase studies where demographic capture is deemed low-yield</cite>. <cite id="fbf58093-3">Global trials face additional challenges: some sites or regions either lack protected-characteristic categories or restrict collection, leading to missing race/ethnicity data</cite>. <cite id="fbf58093-4">Even when standardized categories are used, ethnicity reporting is highly heterogeneous across countries; Latin America shows notable “American Indian or Alaska Native” proportions, while Europe and Asia report near-uniform “White” race, underscoring the operational difficulty of consistent global collection</cite>.
- Definitions and operationalization: <cite id="fbf58093-0">Variations in definitions and collection practices across studies lead to incomplete or non-standardized data; sponsors may drift to local categories or omit fields where race/ethnicity is not material to primary endpoints</cite>. <cite id="fbf58093-2">FDA recommends minimum race and ethnicity categories, but reviews show some approvals did not report enrollment for all recommended categories; missingness may reflect no patients in a group or global restrictions on collecting protected characteristics, and subgroup analyses are often underpowered</cite>. <cite id="fbf58093-3">Recent OMB updates (effective March 28, 2024) further align with FDA-proposed requirements, adding complexity for sponsors who must harmonize domestic and international systems</cite>.

NIH-funded studies: enablers aligned with public-mission incentives
- Accountability and dissemination requirements: <cite id="fbf58093-1">NIH policy requires NIH-funded studies to report race/ethnicity on ClinicalTrials.gov; analyses of 58,000+ trials show study characteristics (e.g., NIH funding) are strongly associated with reporting</cite>. <cite id="fb1656b1-0">Within oncology, NIH funding is associated with the most consistent reporting of race and ethnicity</cite>, indicating that public-mandated transparency and peer review can increase the salience of demographic reporting.
- NIH data lock statements and public accountability: <cite id="fbf58093-0">NIH’s 2016 rule for registration and results reporting mandates demographic fields, and NIH has long promoted inclusion guidance and data sharing</cite>, creating clearer sponsor-level accountability for academic/NIH-led protocols and data systems.
- Research community norms: <cite id="fb1656b1-2">Pediatric NIH trials still underreport in publications and registries, but the direction of change and visibility of race/ethnicity in protocols and publications are generally higher than in industry settings</cite>, suggesting that public funding aligns with norms of transparent inclusion and subgroup reporting, even if gaps persist.

Enforcement and institutional frictions that maintain disparities
- Inconsistent definitions and local variability: <cite id="fbf58093-0">Across institutions and countries, definitions and collection methods for race/ethnicity vary, contributing to incomplete and non-standardized data</cite>. <cite id="fbf58093-3">Updated OMB standards and FDA proposals add to the burden of harmonization; sponsors face alignment challenges between domestic and global sites, with some regions restricting collection of protected characteristics</cite>.
- Sponsor-level accountability and resources: <cite id="fbf58093-0">Despite policies, compliance and enforcement have been inconsistent; sponsors and researchers may lack resources or accountability to implement reporting rigorously</cite>. <cite id="fb1656b1-3">Industry-driven homogeneity incentives and limited perceived utility of small-sample subgroup reporting can further erode compliance</cite>. <cite id="fbf58093-2">FDA’s R/E PMR/C is rare and often constrained by small subgroup sizes, reducing direct financial or regulatory pressure to collect and report comprehensive race/ethnicity data</cite>.
- Multi-regulator context: <cite id="359bcb79-0">NIH, Common Rule, and FDA requirements can co-exist and, where sponsors operate across multiple jurisdictions, differing expectations may lead to minimal data collection to satisfy “some” standard rather than the most complete approach</cite>. <cite id="359bcb79-0">Ambiguity around sIRB reliance exceptions across NIH, OHRP, and FDA proposals adds administrative burden and can slow implementation of uniform data collection practices</cite>.

What would close or narrow the gap
- Harmonized standards and clear operational guidance: <cite id="fbf58093-3">Adopting and enforcing updated federal categories (OMB 2024) aligned with FDA requirements reduces ambiguity and supports common data elements usable across domestic and international sites</cite>. <cite id="fbf58093-4">Developing global, multistakeholder-category schemes that respect local contexts can improve completeness in multinational trials</cite>.
- Strengthen sponsor accountability and incentives: <cite id="fb1656b1-1">FDA and NIH could further tie review or funding decisions to robust race/ethnicity subgroup reporting plans and post-hoc analyses, as seen in PMR/Cs but more broadly</cite>. <cite id="fbf58093-2">Increasing use of R/E PMR/Cs where meaningful heterogeneity is plausible provides regulatory leverage to require comprehensive collection and reporting</cite>.
- Align IRB and regulatory pathways: <cite id="359bcb79-0">Clear guidance on how NIH, Common Rule, and FDA requirements interact—especially for sIRB reliance and exceptions—would streamline compliance for multi-site and multi-sponsor trials common in industry</cite>.
- Build capacity and reduce burden: <cite id="fbf58093-0">Sponsors should standardize eConsent and eCOA instruments to include demographic modules with optional sensitive fields, address privacy concerns, and integrate with trial data platforms to reduce duplication and participant burden</cite>. <cite id="fb1656b1-1">Policies should recognize that smaller trials underreport demographics and provide lighter-touch but consistent requirements and templates to improve completeness</cite>.

Uncertainties and outlook
- The direction is improving but uneven: <cite id="fb1656b1-1">Race reporting across trials has increased modestly over time, but fewer than a quarter report all five groups; industry funding remains a strong predictor of lower reporting</cite>. <cite id="fb1656b1-0">Ethnicity reporting lags race reporting in industry, even as it rises in NIH-funded research</cite>. 
- Definitions and globalization complicate convergence: <cite id="fbf58093-4">Race/ethnicity categories lack global fit; solutions require multistakeholder input and may necessitate relaxing or reinterpreting categories to maintain relevance and comparability</cite>. 
- Evolving FDA/OMB rules: <cite id="fbf58093-3">OMB’s 2024 effective date and FDA’s proposed requirements create near-term alignment pressure</cite>; their implementation could raise baseline reporting completeness if consistently enforced across sponsors.

Bottom line
Identical federal mandates establish the floor for race/ethnicity reporting, but industry trials operate under tighter time, cost, and homogeneity incentives, more fragmented regulatory pathways, and greater heterogeneity in global conduct. <cite id="fb1656b1-1">These factors produce lower reporting and representation in industry-funded studies relative to NIH-funded trials despite shared mandates</cite>. <cite id="fb1656b1-0">NIH funding, coupled with public accountability and inclusion norms, yields more consistent demographic capture in academic-led studies, even where gaps persist</cite>. Convergence will require harmonized standards, stronger sponsor-level incentives and guidance, and practical support to reduce burden and privacy concerns, especially in small and global trials. <cite id="fbf58093-0">Without these measures, compliance will remain uneven and enforcement inconsistent, sustaining disparities in reporting and in who is studied</cite>.

Title: Race/ethnicity reporting and representation in US clinical trials: a cohort study
Snippet: In our analysis of two decades of data from over 20,000 USA-based clinical trials registered in ClinicalTrials. gov, we found that fewer than 44% of trials report any race/ethnicity data. Among trials that do report race/ ethnicity, as a group minorities remain underrepresented compared to their US populations, though at the subgroup level median Black enrollment is not statistically below their US population. Even after controlling for other trial features and conducting several sensitivity analyses evaluating alternative encodings of race/ethnicity, we found that industry-funded trials were associated with less race/ethnicity reporting and with lower rates of minority race/ethnicity enrollment compared to US government-funded trials. 

While the increase in race/ethnicity reporting is encouraging, it constitutes a low bar with fewer than 25% of trials reporting enrollment data for all five major race/ethnicity groups, in contrast with rates of sex reporting, which remained above 99% for all study years. 19 Reporting progress is further complicated by the large subset of completed trials (excluded from this analysis) that have not reported any trial results. Decades of research have highlighted the clinical and ethical concerns presented by selective reporting of trial results (despite legal reporting obligations for many trials). 23 ur data showed that smaller trials were less likely to report race/ethnicity data. While this may reflect trialists' assessment of the limited utility of tracking small populations within limited studies, the absence of transparent trial demographics obscures the generalizability of results and weakens the medical community's ability to identify gaps or opportunities for further research. 

Our results suggest the lack of consensus among previous studies that examined race/ethnicity reporting rates (ranging 2-58% in one review 2 ) may stem from a lack of power and/or differences among their sampled populations. For example, Kwiatkowski et al. found significantly improved race/ethnicity reporting over time in their study of 304 Phase 3, non-industry trials, 10 whereas Loree et al. found only minimal reporting changes in their study of 230 drug approval trials with 97% industry funding. 11 Our model showed industry funding was strongly associated with lower levels of reporting, which may explain the modest findings observed in the drug approval trials. Many studies do not state the funding mix of the trials in their samples, nor the mix of other features that may influence reporting rates.

Title: An Evaluation of Novel Oncology Approvals with a PMR/C for Assessing Data in Racial and Ethnic Populations Underrepresented in Premarket Clinical Trials
Snippet: Despite efforts to standardize and improve transparency in reporting of demographic data for novel drugs (e.g., Clinical Trial Snapshots) there continues to be variable reporting of race and ethnicity data. For reporting of race, FDA recommends sponsors include, at a minimum, options to select AI/AN, Asian, Black or African American, NHPI and White, as well as directions clarifying that one or more of these may be selected (2). This analysis showed some reviews did not report enrollment for all recommended race and ethnicity categories, which may have been due to the timing of data collection for the clinical trials or because there were no patients who identified as the missing races or ethnicities; however, in some cases zero was reported if this was true. White and Asian were the only two demographic categories assessed that were reported in all review documents. Most trials included in this analysis were conducted globally, so the missing data may be related to global restrictions related to protected characteristics, such as race and ethnicity, that prevent collection and reporting of these data (11,12). Among the 20 trials that included information on U.S. enrollment, trials for drugs with a R/E PMR/C had an average U.S. enrollment of 40.9% (12%-73%). In contrast, trials for drugs without a R/E PMR/C reported a higher average U.S. enrollment rate of 66.2% (14.9%-100%). Notably, there were four drugs supported by trials that enrolled only U.S. patients and these drugs did not receive a R/E PMR/C. 

Another factor influencing whether FDA issues a R/E PMR/C is the presence of potential safety signals observed in subgroup analyses. Review documents posted in support of drug approvals often include subgroup analyses that assess whether there are differences in efficacy, safety, PK, and dosing based on intrinsic factors such as race and ethnicity. Review documents for drugs with a R/E PMR/C and those without a R/E PMR/C indicated subgroup analyses are often limited by small sample sizes and/or are incorporated as secondary/exploratory analyses, limiting the ability to draw conclusions about whether meaningful differences in efficacy, safety  dosing, or PK exist across racial and ethnic subgroups.

Title: Race and Ethnicity in Heart Failure Trials: Time to Update Recommended Categories for Global Relevance
Snippet: Background The collection of race and ethnicity data in clinical trials using standardized categories is recommended by the US Food and Drug Administration, although this is primarily for domestic reasons. The applicability and understanding of the categories in multinational trials are uncertain. Methods We analyzed patient‐level data from 13 major heart failure trials, examining race and ethnicity data recorded by country, as recommended by the Food and Drug Administration: “American Indian or Alaska Native,” “Asian,” “Black or African American,” “Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander,” and “White” for race and “Hispanic or Latino” as a minimum for ethnicity (with an expanded list of ethnicities available). Results Of the 54 087 patients studied, approximately 32.3% were women. In the United States, 77% of patients were reported to be of White race and 19% of Black race with very few assigned to another race category (1% Asian, 0.7% Native American, 0.2% Native Hawaiian or other Pacific islander, and 1.4% “other”). In Europe, race was almost uniformly reported as White, and a similar racial homogeneity was reported in Asia (Asian race). Conversely, in Latin America, 8.9% of patients were described as “American Indian or Alaska Native,” with a very high proportion in specific countries (eg, 36% in Guatemala and 21% in Mexico). In the United States, 6.2% of participants were reported to have Hispanic/Latino ethnicity but most patients in Latin America were reported to have this ethnicity; conversely, few patients had this ethnicity reported outside the Americas, including in Spain and Portugal. Among patients designated as Asian race, specific ethnicities (eg, Indian, Japanese etc) almost completely overlapped with the country of origin. Conclusions This study highlights the challenges of applying standardized race and, particularly, ethnicity categories in global clinical trials. A multistakeholder approach is needed to improve the collection of race and ethnicity data in clinical trials.

Title: Implementation of single IRB review for multisite human subjects research: Persistent challenges and possible solutions
Snippet: Workshop participants stressed the need for additional guidance from the NIH and the Office of Human Research Protections (OHRP). There are several differences between the NIH policy and the Common Rule requirement that have led to confusion within institutions. For example, the Common Rule requirement applies to "cooperative research" whereas the NIH policy refers to "multi-site studies where each site will conduct the same protocol." To illustrate, workshop participants indicated that a study in which each site conducts distinct activities as part of a single project (e.g., one site does only imaging, another only biospecimen analysis, another enrolls participants), might be considered cooperative research subject to the Common Rule requirement yet not fall under the scope of the NIH policy. Moreover, the exceptions to the requirement for single IRB review issued by NIH and OHRP do not align, adding to the confusion as institutions try to comply. For example, NIH provides categorical exceptions and has the ability to provide exceptions for individual studies on a case by case basis, whereas OHRP issues only categorical exceptions. 

Further, studies may fall under the oversight of multiple regulatory bodies and agencies. An NIH-funded investigator-initiated study of an investigational medical product would have to comply with NIH policy, the Common Rule, and applicable FDA regulations. While at this time the FDA has not adopted an sIRB requirement, a recent notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) signals their intent to align [8]. While the final rule may change, the NPRM suggests that the forthcoming FDA requirement will differ from both the NIH and Common Rule sIRB requirements. For example, if adopted as proposed in the NPRM, the FDA sIRB requirement will not apply to research that is not conducted under an Investigational New Drug (IND) application or for device studies subject only to the abbreviated Investigational Device Exemption (IDE) requirements. However, those same studies may be subject to the Common Rule and/or NIH sIRB requirements. Guidance is needed as to how these policies work together and what institutions are to do when there appear to be conflicting requirements.
