Title: Patenting Race in a Genomic Age1
Snippet: The racialization of patent law can only fully be understood when viewed in relation to broader federal initiatives that shape the production and use of racial 8 categories in biomedical research. Prominent among these are a wide array of federal mandates that dictate the characterization and application of genetically-based biomedical interventions, such as pharmaceuticals and diagnostic tests, in relation to socially defined categories of race. Key federal mandates include: the National Institutes of Health (NIH) Revitalization Act of 1993, which directed the NIH to establish guidelines for inclusion of women and minorities in clinical research 9 ; the Food and Drug Modernization Act of 1997, which, in the context of drug development, directed that "the Secretary [of Health and Human Services] shall, in consultation with the Director of the NIH and with representatives of the drug manufacturing industry, review and develop guidance, as appropriate, on the inclusion of women and minorities in clinical trials", and two subsequent FDA "Guidances for Industry". The first, a 1999 guidance titled "Population Pharmacokinetics", made recommendations on the use of population pharmacokinetics in the drug development process to help identify differences in drug safety and efficacy among population subgroups, including race and ethnicity 10 ; and the second, a 2005 guidance entitled "Collection of Race and Ethnicity Data in Clinical Trials", which recommends a standardized approach for collecting and reporting race and ethnicity information in clinical trials that produce data for applications to the FDA for drug approval. 

11 Underlying the standardization of data collection in all of these mandates is the Office of Management and Budget's Revised Directive 15 on "Standards for Maintaining, Collecting, and Presenting Federal Data on Race and Ethnicity". 12 The standards were developed "to provide a common language for uniformity and comparability in the collection and use of data on race and ethnicity by Federal agencies". The standards set forth the following basic racial categories for organizing such data: American Indian or Alaska Native, Asian, Black or African American, Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander, and White. There are two categories for data on ethnicity: "Hispanic or Latino", and "Not Hispanic or Latino". 13 Sociologist Michael Omi observes, "Directive 15 has become the de facto standard for state and local agencies, the private and nonprofit sectors, and the research community". 14

Title: Implementation of single IRB review for multisite human subjects research: Persistent challenges and possible solutions
Snippet: In 2016, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) announced a new policy requiring the use of a single IRB (sIRB) for the review of most NIH-funded, multisite human subjects research [1]. The policy became effective in January 2018 and was soon followed by a similar mandate that was incorporated into the revised Common Rule (45 CFR 46.114). The primary rationale provided by both NIH and the Office of Human Research Protections (OHRP) to justify the sIRB requirement was to streamline the review process and eliminate inefficiencies inherent in a duplicative review process while not compromising human participant protections [1,2]. 

To facilitate the implementation of the sIRB requirement, in July 2016, the National Center for the Advancement of Translational Sciences (NCATS), a center within NIH, funded a collaborative effort to support the national adoption of sIRB review, termed Streamlined, Multisite, Accelerated Resources for Trials IRB Reliance Platform (SMART IRB) [3]. The SMART IRB platform provides a reliance agreement (the SMART IRB Reliance Agreement), a method for joining as a participating institution, resources, education, and a web-based process for participating institutions and their investigators to request, track, and document study-specific reliance arrangements. As of March 2023, more than 1080 entities are signatories to the SMART IRB Reliance Agreement. 

It is now over 4 years since the implementation of the NIH sIRB policy and more than 2 years since the effective date of the Common Rule requirement. Yet, significant challenges with the implementation of sIRB remain [4][5][6][7]. The leadership of SMART IRB has organized an "Emerging Issues" annual workshop in which leaders in human participant protections gather to discuss sIRB review. The theme of the 2022 workshop was to identify "persistent barriers and future solutions to the success of single IRB." Discussion topics were identified by workshop organizers based upon solicited input from human research protection program (HRPP) leaders throughout the country and from issues raised during discussions at prior SMART IRB talks and workshops. This paper summarizes the proceedings of the workshop.

Summary
Despite overlapping federal mandates, NIH-funded studies and industry-sponsored trials differ in their incentives, governance, and operational context for collecting and reporting race/ethnicity, which helps explain the lower reporting and representation in industry trials. <cite id="fb1656b1-1">Across two decades of >20,000 US-based trials, industry-funded studies were associated with less race/ethnicity reporting and lower minority enrollment than US government-funded trials, even after controlling for other features</cite>. <cite id="fb1656b1-0">Within tumor therapies, NIH-funded studies were the most consistent reporters of race and ethnicity, while industry-funded trials showed an upward trend in race reporting but not ethnicity reporting</cite>. These differences are not due to the absence of mandates: <cite id="359bcb79-2">federal initiatives since the 1990s, including OMB standards and FDA guidance, standardize race/ethnicity categories and expect sponsors to collect and report such data for regulatory applications</cite>, and <cite id="fbf58093-1">NIH policy since 2017 requires NIH-funded studies to report race/ethnicity on ClinicalTrials.gov</cite>. Below, we synthesize why compliance and completeness still diverge.

What the mandates require and how they apply differently
- NIH/Common Rule and FDA set the baseline requirements. <cite id="359bcb79-2">The NIH Revitalization Act (1993), FDA guidance (1999 and 2005), and OMB standards collectively require standardized collection and reporting of race/ethnicity in biomedical research and drug development</cite>, providing the common categories (race: American Indian/Alaska Native, Asian, Black or African American, Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander, White; ethnicity: Hispanic/Latino vs. Not Hispanic/Latino). <cite id="fbf58093-0">NIH’s 2016 final rule for clinical trial registration and results reporting mandates demographic characteristics—including race and ethnicity—on ClinicalTrials.gov</cite>. <cite id="359bcb79-3">FDA’s guidance emphasizes enhanced diversity and standardization of race/ethnicity data collection for trials that support labeling and approvals</cite>.
- Despite identical “identical” mandates, scope and enforcement differ by setting. <cite id="359bcb79-0">An NIH-funded investigator-initiated study must meet NIH policy, the Common Rule, and applicable FDA regulations; FDA has proposed—and may implement—an investigator/IDE-exempt sIRB rule that would differ from both NIH and the Common Rule, creating practical ambiguity in how policies interplay</cite>. <cite id="359bcb79-0">NIH and OHRP exceptions to single-IRB reliance do not fully align, and multiple regulatory bodies may co-oversight, complicating compliance pathways</cite>. These administrative frictions can slow or dilute implementation in complex, multi-sponsor contexts that are common in industry consortia.

Empirical differences in reporting and representation
- Industry vs. NIH: <cite id="fb1656b1-1">A cohort study of 20,000+ trials found fewer than 44% reported any race/ethnicity data overall, and industry-funded trials had lower race/ethnicity reporting and lower minority enrollment than government-funded trials, even after conditioning on other trial features</cite>. <cite id="fb1656b1-3">Analyses of enrollment also suggest industry sponsorship is associated with greater White enrollment, potentially reflecting regulatory and financial incentives that reduce perceived confounding from patient-related factors, while showing smaller but positive trends for Latino enrollment relative to government-funded trials</cite>. <cite id="fb1656b1-0">In glioma therapy trials, NIH-funded studies were the most consistent in reporting both race and ethnicity; industry-sponsored trials improved over time for race but not ethnicity</cite>.
- NIH studies still have gaps: <cite id="fb1656b1-2">In pediatric NIH-funded trials, reporting of race/ethnicity remains incomplete across publications and ClinicalTrials.gov</cite>, indicating that mandates alone do not guarantee universal capture.

Organizational and incentive-based reasons specific to industry trials
- Sponsor control and financial incentives: <cite id="fb1656b1-3">Industry sponsorship is associated with enrollment patterns that may reflect regulatory and financial incentives favoring homogeneity to reduce risk of confounding, which can indirectly discourage detailed demographic reporting and recruitment of heterogeneous groups</cite>. <cite id="fbf58093-2">FDA reviewers often find subgroup analyses limited by small samples and treated as secondary/exploratory, which may disincentivize sponsors from investing resources in detailed race/ethnicity stratification unless a regulator flags race/ethnicity as a risk management concern (e.g., via a Race/Ethnicity Pre-Approval Requirement/Caveat, PMR/C)</cite>. <cite id="fb1656b1-3">Only a minority of trials received such PMR/Cs, suggesting limited regulatory leverage to enforce robust subgroup reporting in routine approvals</cite>.
- Publication norms and pressure to publish efficacy: <cite id="fb1656b1-1">Industry-funded trials tend to be less likely to report race/ethnicity demographics than government-funded trials, and smaller trials are less likely to report race/ethnicity at all</cite>. In industry portfolios, emphasis may be placed on time-to-approval and headline efficacy rather than demographic breakdowns that are ancillary to peer review or investor audiences, reducing perceived value and priority for comprehensive demographic capture. <cite id="fbf58093-0">Sponsors and researchers may lack accountability or resources to adhere strictly to reporting standards, and privacy concerns can impede participant willingness to disclose race/ethnicity</cite>.
- Trial design and scale: <cite id="fb1656b1-1">Smaller trials are less likely to report race/ethnicity demographics; industry sponsors run many smaller, global, or early-phase studies where demographic capture is deemed low-yield</cite>. <cite id="fbf58093-3">Global trials face additional challenges: some sites or regions either lack protected-characteristic categories or restrict collection, leading to missing race/ethnicity data</cite>. <cite id="fbf58093-4">Even when standardized categories are used, ethnicity reporting is highly heterogeneous across countries; Latin America shows notable “American Indian or Alaska Native” proportions, while Europe and Asia report near-uniform “White” race, underscoring the operational difficulty of consistent global collection</cite>.
- Definitions and operationalization: <cite id="fbf58093-0">Variations in definitions and collection practices across studies lead to incomplete or non-standardized data; sponsors may drift to local categories or omit fields where race/ethnicity is not material to primary endpoints</cite>. <cite id="fbf58093-2">FDA recommends minimum race and ethnicity categories, but reviews show some approvals did not report enrollment for all recommended categories; missingness may reflect no patients in a group or global restrictions on collecting protected characteristics, and subgroup analyses are often underpowered</cite>. <cite id="fbf58093-3">Recent OMB updates (effective March 28, 2024) further align with FDA-proposed requirements, adding complexity for sponsors who must harmonize domestic and international systems</cite>.

NIH-funded studies: enablers aligned with public-mission incentives
- Accountability and dissemination requirements: <cite id="fbf58093-1">NIH policy requires NIH-funded studies to report race/ethnicity on ClinicalTrials.gov; analyses of 58,000+ trials show study characteristics (e.g., NIH funding) are strongly associated with reporting</cite>. <cite id="fb1656b1-0">Within oncology, NIH funding is associated with the most consistent reporting of race and ethnicity</cite>, indicating that public-mandated transparency and peer review can increase the salience of demographic reporting.
- NIH data lock statements and public accountability: <cite id="fbf58093-0">NIH’s 2016 rule for registration and results reporting mandates demographic fields, and NIH has long promoted inclusion guidance and data sharing</cite>, creating clearer sponsor-level accountability for academic/NIH-led protocols and data systems.
- Research community norms: <cite id="fb1656b1-2">Pediatric NIH trials still underreport in publications and registries, but the direction of change and visibility of race/ethnicity in protocols and publications are generally higher than in industry settings</cite>, suggesting that public funding aligns with norms of transparent inclusion and subgroup reporting, even if gaps persist.

Enforcement and institutional frictions that maintain disparities
- Inconsistent definitions and local variability: <cite id="fbf58093-0">Across institutions and countries, definitions and collection methods for race/ethnicity vary, contributing to incomplete and non-standardized data</cite>. <cite id="fbf58093-3">Updated OMB standards and FDA proposals add to the burden of harmonization; sponsors face alignment challenges between domestic and global sites, with some regions restricting collection of protected characteristics</cite>.
- Sponsor-level accountability and resources: <cite id="fbf58093-0">Despite policies, compliance and enforcement have been inconsistent; sponsors and researchers may lack resources or accountability to implement reporting rigorously</cite>. <cite id="fb1656b1-3">Industry-driven homogeneity incentives and limited perceived utility of small-sample subgroup reporting can further erode compliance</cite>. <cite id="fbf58093-2">FDA’s R/E PMR/C is rare and often constrained by small subgroup sizes, reducing direct financial or regulatory pressure to collect and report comprehensive race/ethnicity data</cite>.
- Multi-regulator context: <cite id="359bcb79-0">NIH, Common Rule, and FDA requirements can co-exist and, where sponsors operate across multiple jurisdictions, differing expectations may lead to minimal data collection to satisfy “some” standard rather than the most complete approach</cite>. <cite id="359bcb79-0">Ambiguity around sIRB reliance exceptions across NIH, OHRP, and FDA proposals adds administrative burden and can slow implementation of uniform data collection practices</cite>.

What would close or narrow the gap
- Harmonized standards and clear operational guidance: <cite id="fbf58093-3">Adopting and enforcing updated federal categories (OMB 2024) aligned with FDA requirements reduces ambiguity and supports common data elements usable across domestic and international sites</cite>. <cite id="fbf58093-4">Developing global, multistakeholder-category schemes that respect local contexts can improve completeness in multinational trials</cite>.
- Strengthen sponsor accountability and incentives: <cite id="fb1656b1-1">FDA and NIH could further tie review or funding decisions to robust race/ethnicity subgroup reporting plans and post-hoc analyses, as seen in PMR/Cs but more broadly</cite>. <cite id="fbf58093-2">Increasing use of R/E PMR/Cs where meaningful heterogeneity is plausible provides regulatory leverage to require comprehensive collection and reporting</cite>.
- Align IRB and regulatory pathways: <cite id="359bcb79-0">Clear guidance on how NIH, Common Rule, and FDA requirements interact—especially for sIRB reliance and exceptions—would streamline compliance for multi-site and multi-sponsor trials common in industry</cite>.
- Build capacity and reduce burden: <cite id="fbf58093-0">Sponsors should standardize eConsent and eCOA instruments to include demographic modules with optional sensitive fields, address privacy concerns, and integrate with trial data platforms to reduce duplication and participant burden</cite>. <cite id="fb1656b1-1">Policies should recognize that smaller trials underreport demographics and provide lighter-touch but consistent requirements and templates to improve completeness</cite>.

Uncertainties and outlook
- The direction is improving but uneven: <cite id="fb1656b1-1">Race reporting across trials has increased modestly over time, but fewer than a quarter report all five groups; industry funding remains a strong predictor of lower reporting</cite>. <cite id="fb1656b1-0">Ethnicity reporting lags race reporting in industry, even as it rises in NIH-funded research</cite>. 
- Definitions and globalization complicate convergence: <cite id="fbf58093-4">Race/ethnicity categories lack global fit; solutions require multistakeholder input and may necessitate relaxing or reinterpreting categories to maintain relevance and comparability</cite>. 
- Evolving FDA/OMB rules: <cite id="fbf58093-3">OMB’s 2024 effective date and FDA’s proposed requirements create near-term alignment pressure</cite>; their implementation could raise baseline reporting completeness if consistently enforced across sponsors.

Bottom line
Identical federal mandates establish the floor for race/ethnicity reporting, but industry trials operate under tighter time, cost, and homogeneity incentives, more fragmented regulatory pathways, and greater heterogeneity in global conduct. <cite id="fb1656b1-1">These factors produce lower reporting and representation in industry-funded studies relative to NIH-funded trials despite shared mandates</cite>. <cite id="fb1656b1-0">NIH funding, coupled with public accountability and inclusion norms, yields more consistent demographic capture in academic-led studies, even where gaps persist</cite>. Convergence will require harmonized standards, stronger sponsor-level incentives and guidance, and practical support to reduce burden and privacy concerns, especially in small and global trials. <cite id="fbf58093-0">Without these measures, compliance will remain uneven and enforcement inconsistent, sustaining disparities in reporting and in who is studied</cite>. </answer>

Title: A Cross-Sectional Analysis of Interventional Clinical Trials in High-Grade Glioma Therapy
Snippet: We identified the majority of studies were funded privately ("Other", 120; 59.7%), followed by industry-funded (40; 19.9%) and NIH-funded (36; 17.9%) studies (Table 1). We grouped the studies according to the type of institution that performed each trial. The majority were completed by private academic and business ventures (72; 35.8%), followed by studies conducted by both public and private entities ("Mixed", 54; 26.9%). We then compared trial reporting of enrolled participant demographics stratified by their funding source. We found the overall most consistent reporters of both race and ethnicity to be NIH-funded across all years, followed by private/third-party-funded trials ("Other") with an upward trend over time (Figure 3E,F). Industry-funded trials also demonstrated a strong upward trend in race reporting, but not ethnicity reporting, over time. Network-funded trials showed 100% reporting, although the sample size was relatively small (five, 2.5%).

Title: Race/ethnicity reporting and representation in US clinical trials: a cohort study
Snippet: In our analysis of two decades of data from over 20,000 USA-based clinical trials registered in ClinicalTrials. gov, we found that fewer than 44% of trials report any race/ethnicity data. Among trials that do report race/ ethnicity, as a group minorities remain underrepresented compared to their US populations, though at the subgroup level median Black enrollment is not statistically below their US population. Even after controlling for other trial features and conducting several sensitivity analyses evaluating alternative encodings of race/ethnicity, we found that industry-funded trials were associated with less race/ethnicity reporting and with lower rates of minority race/ethnicity enrollment compared to US government-funded trials. 

While the increase in race/ethnicity reporting is encouraging, it constitutes a low bar with fewer than 25% of trials reporting enrollment data for all five major race/ethnicity groups, in contrast with rates of sex reporting, which remained above 99% for all study years. 19 Reporting progress is further complicated by the large subset of completed trials (excluded from this analysis) that have not reported any trial results. Decades of research have highlighted the clinical and ethical concerns presented by selective reporting of trial results (despite legal reporting obligations for many trials). 23 ur data showed that smaller trials were less likely to report race/ethnicity data. While this may reflect trialists' assessment of the limited utility of tracking small populations within limited studies, the absence of transparent trial demographics obscures the generalizability of results and weakens the medical community's ability to identify gaps or opportunities for further research. 

Our results suggest the lack of consensus among previous studies that examined race/ethnicity reporting rates (ranging 2-58% in one review 2 ) may stem from a lack of power and/or differences among their sampled populations. For example, Kwiatkowski et al. found significantly improved race/ethnicity reporting over time in their study of 304 Phase 3, non-industry trials, 10 whereas Loree et al. found only minimal reporting changes in their study of 230 drug approval trials with 97% industry funding. 11 Our model showed industry funding was strongly associated with lower levels of reporting, which may explain the modest findings observed in the drug approval trials. Many studies do not state the funding mix of the trials in their samples, nor the mix of other features that may influence reporting rates.

Title: Reporting and Representation of Participant Race and Ethnicity in National Institutes of Health–Funded Pediatric Clinical Trials
Snippet: This cross-sectional study assesses reporting of race and ethnicity in National Institutes of Health (NIH)–funded pediatric clinical trials in publications and ClinicalTrials.gov.

Title: Race/ethnicity reporting and representation in US clinical trials: a cohort study
Snippet: On ClinicalTrials.gov "Not Applicable" is used to describe trials and Drug Administration-defined phases, including trials of devices or behavioral interventions. Funding categories were determined with data on the sponsor and collaborators. Industry funding includes trials with an industry sponsor or collaborating agency US Government trials include remaining trials with a US Government sponsor or collaborating agency. underrepresented populations. However, these trials comprise a narrow subset (total US participants were approximately 103,000, compared to the approximate 2,0878,000 in our study) and apply only to studies for new molecular entities or biologics (i.e. does not include trials for expanded indications, off-label use, or non pharmacologic interventions). In our cohort 21% of trials reported 0 Black enrollees, indicative of the heterogeneity that can be obscured in smaller samples. 

Similar to reporting, the inconsistent results among previous studies assessing trial diversity is likely influenced by the varying mixture of trial features (e.g. funding) present within their samples. Detection of minority enrollment trends is also more challenging because only a fraction of trials report race/ethnicity enrollments (especially for all five groups) and the trends' true effect sizes are likely modest as demonstrated in our analysis. Our findings begin to resolve these inconsistencies, but without complete race/ethnicity reporting, all estimates remain susceptible to reporting bias. 

The association of industry with greater White enrollment may result from both regulatory and financial incentives that indirectly reward homogeneity through the reduced risk of confounding from patientrelated factors (e.g. more predictable therapeutic effects, decreased risk of adverse events). 7 As industry contributes the most to applied preclinical and clinical research in addition to production, marketing and distribution of new therapies, 28 this finding may have unique implications for disparities in treatment efficacy and access. Interestingly, industry and academic funding trended toward a positive effect among Latinos relative to government funding. We suspect this may reflect a unique barrier to recruitment of Latinos compared to other minorities among US Government trials. Relative to US Government-funded trials, the association of academic funding with race/ethnicity enrollment was similar to though typically weaker than that of industry.

Title: Defining the Race and Ethnic Standards for Federal Statistics and Administrative Reporting
Snippet: s clinical trial did not clearly show that the drug worked better in African Americans, as it relied on "self-identified" African Americans and lacked a comparison group (Kahn 2007). Bidil is a concrete example of how the sociocultural factors in disease may be ignored with the current assumption of a race and presumed genetic difference (Brody and Hunt 2006). This is further detrimental since race-based categories in clinical trials ignore the heterogeneous composition of racial groups (Yudell et al. 2016).

As currently presented, the NIH and FDA follow federal reporting of race and ethnicity in their studies. Both agencies contribute largely to American health and the training of our biomedical workforce, e.g., NIH training grants (T32) and fellowships (F30, F31-Diversity) (NIH Individual Fellowships 2021; NIH Institutional Training Grants 2021). Enforcing a new definition to race at the federal level may cause downstream confusion among states, particularly among educational and medical systems that benefit from NIH and FDA funding. In this memorandum, we explore the possible outcomes of two policy options: 1) alter the Information Quality Act Guidelines, and 2) include the definition of race in the Race and Ethnic Standards for Federal Statistics and Administrative Reporting. We also explore inaction as a model to support clarity and the importance of our recommendations.

Title: Reporting and representation of race and ethnicity data in phase III clinical trials for hematological malignancies
Snippet: Various policies and guidelines have been issued regarding the reporting of race and ethnicity data for the Us National institutes of health (Nih)-funded trial participants since 1990s [14]. this effort has been supported by multiple academic and governmental initiatives [14]. in 2016, the Nih introduced a final rule requiring the registration and submission of results information for clinical trials, which mandates that demographic characteristics, including race and ethnicity, be reported in clinicaltrials.gov [15]. Despite these policies and guidelines in place for decades, the reporting of race and ethnicity data in clinical trials remains insufficient, and enforcement and compliance have been inconsistent. some sponsors and researchers may lack accountability or resources to adhere strictly to reporting standards. trial participants may be reluctant to disclose their sensitive personal information, including race and ethnicity data, given data security and privacy concerns [16]. 

Variations in race and ethnicity definition and collection across studies can also contribute to incomplete or non-standardized data collection. additionally, guidelines and regulations concerning racial and ethnic reporting may vary by country, institution, or even within the same trial. thus in June 2024, the Us FDa released a guidance to enhance the enrollment of underrepresented populations in clinical trials [9]. Nowadays it remains a significant challenge to achieve adequate representation of each racial and ethnic population in trials [17]. Our previous research found that non-White racial and ethnic minorities were underrepresented in clinical trials for solid tumors [18]. in our current study, a similar pattern was observed-a substantial majority of participants in trials for hematological malignancies were White (76.3%), while smaller proportions were reported for Black/african american, american indian/alaska Native, asian, and Native hawaiian/Other Pacific islander, which also aligns with earlier findings in this area [6,[19][20][21][22]. Title: Race and Ethnicity in Heart Failure Trials: Time to Update Recommended Categories for Global Relevance
Snippet: Background The collection of race and ethnicity data in clinical trials using standardized categories is recommended by the US Food and Drug Administration, although this is primarily for domestic reasons. The applicability and understanding of the categories in multinational trials are uncertain. Methods We analyzed patient‐level data from 13 major heart failure trials, examining race and ethnicity data recorded by country, as recommended by the Food and Drug Administration: “American Indian or Alaska Native,” “Asian,” “Black or African American,” “Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander,” and “White” for race and “Hispanic or Latino” as a minimum for ethnicity (with an expanded list of ethnicities available). Results Of the 54 087 patients studied, approximately 32.3% were women. In the United States, 77% of patients were reported to be of White race and 19% of Black race with very few assigned to another race category (1% Asian, 0.7% Native American, 0.2% Native Hawaiian or other Pacific islander, and 1.4% “other”). In Europe, race was almost uniformly reported as White, and a similar racial homogeneity was reported in Asia (Asian race). Conversely, in Latin America, 8.9% of patients were described as “American Indian or Alaska Native,” with a very high proportion in specific countries (eg, 36% in Guatemala and 21% in Mexico). In the United States, 6.2% of participants were reported to have Hispanic/Latino ethnicity but most patients in Latin America were reported to have this ethnicity; conversely, few patients had this ethnicity reported outside the Americas, including in Spain and Portugal. Among patients designated as Asian race, specific ethnicities (eg, Indian, Japanese etc) almost completely overlapped with the country of origin. Conclusions This study highlights the challenges of applying standardized race and, particularly, ethnicity categories in global clinical trials. A multistakeholder approach is needed to improve the collection of race and ethnicity data in clinical trials.

Title: Implementation of single IRB review for multisite human subjects research: Persistent challenges and possible solutions
Snippet: Workshop participants stressed the need for additional guidance from the NIH and the Office of Human Research Protections (OHRP). There are several differences between the NIH policy and the Common Rule requirement that have led to confusion within institutions. For example, the Common Rule requirement applies to "cooperative research" whereas the NIH policy refers to "multi-site studies where each site will conduct the same protocol." To illustrate, workshop participants indicated that a study in which each site conducts distinct activities as part of a single project (e.g., one site does only imaging, another only biospecimen analysis, another enrolls participants), might be considered cooperative research subject to the Common Rule requirement yet not fall under the scope of the NIH policy. Moreover, the exceptions to the requirement for single IRB review issued by NIH and OHRP do not align, adding to the confusion as institutions try to comply. For example, NIH provides categorical exceptions and has the ability to provide exceptions for individual studies on a case by case basis, whereas OHRP issues only categorical exceptions. 

Further, studies may fall under the oversight of multiple regulatory bodies and agencies. An NIH-funded investigator-initiated study of an investigational medical product would have to comply with NIH policy, the Common Rule, and applicable FDA regulations. While at this time the FDA has not adopted an sIRB requirement, a recent notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) signals their intent to align [8]. While the final rule may change, the NPRM suggests that the forthcoming FDA requirement will differ from both the NIH and Common Rule sIRB requirements. For example, if adopted as proposed in the NPRM, the FDA sIRB requirement will not apply to research that is not conducted under an Investigational New Drug (IND) application or for device studies subject only to the abbreviated Investigational Device Exemption (IDE) requirements. However, those same studies may be subject to the Common Rule and/or NIH sIRB requirements. Guidance is needed as to how these policies work together and what institutions are to do when there appear to be conflicting requirements.

Title: Patenting Race in a Genomic Age1
Snippet: The racialization of patent law can only fully be understood when viewed in relation to broader federal initiatives that shape the production and use of racial 8 categories in biomedical research. Prominent among these are a wide array of federal mandates that dictate the characterization and application of genetically-based biomedical interventions, such as pharmaceuticals and diagnostic tests, in relation to socially defined categories of race. Key federal mandates include: the National Institutes of Health (NIH) Revitalization Act of 1993, which directed the NIH to establish guidelines for inclusion of women and minorities in clinical research 9 ; the Food and Drug Modernization Act of 1997, which, in the context of drug development, directed that "the Secretary [of Health and Human Services] shall, in consultation with the Director of the NIH and with representatives of the drug manufacturing industry, review and develop guidance, as appropriate, on the inclusion of women and minorities in clinical trials", and two subsequent FDA "Guidances for Industry". The first, a 1999 guidance titled "Population Pharmacokinetics", made recommendations on the use of population pharmacokinetics in the drug development process to help identify differences in drug safety and efficacy among population subgroups, including race and ethnicity 10 ; and the second, a 2005 guidance entitled "Collection of Race and Ethnicity Data in Clinical Trials", which recommends a standardized approach for collecting and reporting race and ethnicity information in clinical trials that produce data for applications to the FDA for drug approval. 

11 Underlying the standardization of data collection in all of these mandates is the Office of Management and Budget's Revised Directive 15 on "Standards for Maintaining, Collecting, and Presenting Federal Data on Race and Ethnicity". 12 The standards were developed "to provide a common language for uniformity and comparability in the collection and use of data on race and ethnicity by Federal agencies". snippet.text:
Workshop participants stressed the need for additional guidance from the NIH and the Office of Human Research Protections (OHRP). There are several differences between the NIH policy and the Common Rule requirement that have led to confusion within institutions. For example, the Common Rule requirement applies to "cooperative research" whereas the NIH policy refers to "multi-site studies where each site will conduct the same protocol." To illustrate, workshop participants indicated that a study in which each site conducts distinct activities as part of a single project (e.g., one site does only imaging, another only biospecimen analysis, another enrolls participants), might be considered cooperative research subject to the Common Rule requirement yet not fall under the scope of the NIH policy. Moreover, the exceptions to the requirement for single IRB review issued by NIH and OHRP do not align, adding to the confusion as institutions try to comply. For example, NIH provides categorical exceptions and has the ability to provide exceptions for individual studies on a case by case basis, whereas OHRP issues only categorical exceptions. 

Further, studies may fall under the oversight of multiple regulatory bodies and agencies. An NIH-funded investigator-initiated study of an investigational medical product would have to comply with NIH policy, the Common Rule, and applicable FDA regulations. While at this time the FDA has not adopted an sIRB requirement, a recent notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) signals their intent to align [8]. While the final rule may change, the NPRM suggests that the forthcoming FDA requirement will differ from both the NIH and Common Rule sIRB requirements. For example, if adopted as proposed in the NPRM, the FDA sIRB requirement will not apply to research that is not conducted under an Investigational New Drug (IND) application or for device studies subject only to the abbreviated Investigational Device Exemption (IDE) requirements. However, those same studies may be subject to the Common Rule and/or NIH sIRB requirements. Guidance is needed as to how these policies work together and what institutions are to do when there appear to be conflicting requirements.

Summary
After the 2017 NIH Policy on Inclusion mandated that NIH‑funded studies report race and ethnicity to ClinicalTrials.gov, the overall rate of missing or incomplete demographic reporting declined but persistent underreporting remains attributable to intertwined policy, operational, and system barriers. <cite id="141d96a3-0">Since 2017, the NIH Policy on the Dissemination of NIH‑Funded Clinical Trial Information requires clinical studies to report race and ethnicity information to ClinicalTrials.gov</cite> <cite id="141d96a3-3">In 2009, over 50% of registered studies failed to report race or ethnicity, or both; by 2024, this proportion had fallen to 17%, but observational studies were consistently less likely than interventional trials to report race, ethnicity, or both</cite>.

Policy and incentives: weak enforcement and uneven accountability
- The 2017 policy shifted NIH requirements to prospective dissemination and post‑results reporting on ClinicalTrials.gov, but compliance and accountability mechanisms remain uneven across funders and sponsors. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Despite decades of policies and guidelines, the reporting of race and ethnicity data in clinical trials remains insufficient, and enforcement and compliance have been inconsistent; some sponsors and researchers may lack accountability or resources to adhere strictly to reporting standards</cite> <cite id="141d96a3-3">Previous analyses have shown that trials delay reporting results to ClinicalTrials.gov despite ethical and regulatory mandates; in examples where both registry and peer‑reviewed literature are used, a large proportion have no public results despite concluding more than 7 years prior</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">Less than 44% of US‑based trials reported any race/ethnicity data; industry‑funded trials were strongly associated with lower race/ethnicity reporting compared to US government‑funded trials</cite>. 
- Incentive misalignment persists: visibility and penalties for noncompliance are limited, and sponsors face minimal consequence for incomplete submissions. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Some sponsors and researchers may lack accountability or resources to adhere strictly to reporting standards</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">Industry funding was strongly associated with lower levels of race/ethnicity reporting, consistent with minimal disincentives for sponsors who underreport</cite>. 
- At the regulatory interface, global and cross‑jurisdictional differences reduce pressure to collect locally unnecessary or prohibited data. <cite id="ffc1efd7-1">Missing data in race/ethnicity reporting may be related to global restrictions related to protected characteristics, such as race and ethnicity, that prevent collection and reporting of these data</cite>.

Protocol, IRB/ethics, and consent barriers to data collection
- Ethics and privacy concerns deter collection and explicit consent for sensitive demographic data. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Trial participants may be reluctant to disclose sensitive personal information, including race and ethnicity data, given data security and privacy concerns</cite>. 
- IRB expectations and review practices can discourage detailed demographic capture if categories are not clearly justified or if privacy risks are perceived to be high. <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">The absence of transparent trial demographics is partly due to small sample sizes and trialists’ assessments of limited utility for small populations, but IRB/ethics and consent burdens also shape whether such fields are included</cite>. 
- Protocols often omit clear procedures for race/ethnicity collection, or use ambiguous language, which leads to inconsistent capture at sites. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Variations in race and ethnicity definitions and collection practices across studies contribute to incomplete or non‑standardized data</cite> <cite id="d28ce2dd-0">ClinicalTrials.gov entries showed significant variability in how race/ethnicity was reported, requiring custom parsing; 0.04% had empty tables or ‘NA’ placeholders and 0.9% of 1,000 checked records had structural inconsistencies, necessitating manual adjudication</cite>.

Standardization, denominators, and multilingual/global constraints
- Lack of harmonized definitions and categories across institutions, countries, and trial phases creates “no true negatives” ambiguity and inconsistent denominators, undermining completeness and comparability. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Variations in race and ethnicity definitions and collection across studies can also contribute to incomplete or non‑standardized data collection</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-2">European Union member countries have varying legal definitions of race and ethnic origin; some laws, such as in France, prohibit collecting data that directly or indirectly reveals racial or ethnic origin</cite>. 
- Multilingual and cross‑border recruitment reduces the likelihood of collecting locally sensitive attributes, and sponsors often default to minimal options or omit fields. <cite id="ffc1efd7-1">White and Asian were the only two demographic categories consistently reported across reviews; missing data may be related to global restrictions on protected characteristics, and trials conducted globally often lack enrollment for non‑White groups</cite>. 
- Specialty and trial‑type differences persist, with observational and early‑phase studies less likely to report race/ethnicity, reinforcing heterogeneity in completeness. <cite id="141d96a3-3">Observational studies were consistently less likely than interventional trials to report race, ethnicity, or both; early‑phase trials were among those least likely to report</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-4">Across US phase 3 oncology trials, White participants were overrepresented and racial/ethnic minority groups remained underrepresented</cite>.

Feasibility and capacity: small trials, cost, and perceived utility
- Small sample sizes and limited budgets deter detailed subgroup tabulation and reporting. <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">Smaller trials were less likely to report race/ethnicity; this may reflect limited utility assessments for small populations, but it also reflects cost and resource constraints</cite>. 
- Sponsors face heterogeneous definitions and no single standard output for submission, increasing effort and error, especially for global trials. <cite id="d28ce2dd-0">Significant variability in reporting methods required custom extraction; 0.04% of studies had empty/NA structures and 0.9% of 1,000 checked entries had inconsistencies, with 115 and 27 studies needing manual adjudication</cite>. 
- In oncology and other areas, subgroup analyses are often exploratory with small samples, limiting sponsors’ appetite to invest in race/ethnicity reporting. <cite id="ffc1efd7-1">Review documents for drugs with race/ethnicity Pre‑Market Review Conditions often had subgroup analyses limited by small sample sizes or included as secondary/exploratory analyses, limiting conclusions and potentially discouraging full reporting</cite>.

ClinicalTrials.gov data quality and validation limits
- Even when data are submitted, the registry contains structural and semantic inconsistencies that complicate automated validation and completeness checks. <cite id="d28ce2dd-0">There was significant variability in how race/ethnicity was reported, with some entries using NIH/OMB standards and others custom categories/tables; 0.04% had empty/NA placeholders; 0.9% of 1,000 checked entries had inconsistencies, requiring manual adjudication</cite>. 
- These data quality issues obscure true underrepresentation and create noise in monitoring progress. <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">The absence of transparent demographics in over half of US‑based trials and the even lower fraction reporting all five major groups (fewer than 25%) reflect both collection and submission barriers</cite>.

What has improved, and where gaps remain
- Post‑2017 progress is measurable but incomplete. <cite id="141d96a3-3">Between 2009 and 2024, the share of studies failing to report race/ethnicity fell from over 50% to 17%, though patterns remain uneven by trial type and design</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">Fewer than 44% of US‑based trials reported any race/ethnicity data, and fewer than 25% reported enrollment for all five major groups</cite>. 
- NIH and FDA have continued to refine guidance and incentives, yet representation and reporting do not yet meet equity goals. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">In June 2024, the FDA released guidance to enhance enrollment of underrepresented populations</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-2">Despite challenges, many actions have not yet led to sufficient improvements in diversity and reporting; ethical and regulatory obstacles and operational/financial constraints persist</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-4">Phase 3 cancer trials continue to overrepresent Whites and underrepresent racial/ethnic minorities</cite>.

Why underreporting persists after 2017
- Inconsistent incentives and enforcement: funders and sponsors face low cost of noncompliance, delayed result posting, and limited audit/penalty regimes, weakening implementation. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Enforcement and compliance have been inconsistent; sponsors may lack accountability or resources</cite> <cite id="141d96a3-3">Trials delay reporting results despite mandates</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">Industry funding is strongly associated with lower reporting</cite>.
- Protocol/IRB/consent barriers: privacy concerns, unclear IRB expectations, and absence of clear consent pathways reduce collection of sensitive demographics. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Participants may be reluctant to disclose race/ethnicity due to privacy concerns</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">Trialists’ assessments of limited utility and small trials’ constraints, compounded by ethics/consent burdens, hinder reporting</cite>.
- Lack of harmonized definitions, categories, and denominators: heterogeneous standards and legal prohibitions in some jurisdictions impede consistent capture and submission, especially in global trials. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Variations in definitions and collection practices contribute to incomplete data</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-2">EU/UK legal differences and French prohibitions on collecting race/ethnicity impede data collection</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-1">Global restrictions can prevent collection/reporting, leading to missing categories</cite>.
- Data system and validation limits: registry variability and structural inconsistencies hamper automated capture and verification, creating a tolerance for incomplete submissions. <cite id="d28ce2dd-0">Significant variability and structural inconsistencies in ClinicalTrials.gov entries required manual adjudication, indicating intrinsic data quality limits</cite>.
- Trial‑level feasibility and sponsor priorities: small sample sizes, cost constraints, and the exploratory nature of subgroup analyses reduce sponsor motivation to invest in race/ethnicity collection and reporting. <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">Smaller trials were less likely to report race/ethnicity</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-1">Subgroup analyses are often limited by small samples and treated as exploratory, limiting reporting</cite>.

Practical steps suggested by the evidence
- Align incentives: strengthen NIH/awardee requirements for race/ethnicity collection and publish noncompliance, with funding contingent on transparent demographic reporting and timely results posting. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Improved accountability and resources are needed to adhere to reporting standards</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">Industry‑funded trials’ lower reporting suggests targeted incentives are needed</cite>.
- Standardize definitions and consent: adopt NIH/OMB or FDA‑aligned categories, embed them in templates, and obtain clear participant consent for use in public registries. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Harmonized definitions and collection practices reduce incompleteness</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-2">FDA guidance on determining race and ethnicity has been applied, but legal differences require careful standardization</cite>.
- Reduce IRB/ethics friction: provide ethics‑approved consent scripts and data minimization frameworks that address privacy concerns while enabling necessary demographic capture. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Privacy concerns drive reluctance to disclose race/ethnicity</cite>.
- Support small trials: provide templates, IRB‑approved case report form fields, and sponsor‑side tools to tabulate subgroups at low cost. <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">Small trials are less likely to report demographics; transparent subgroup tabulation remains under‑invested</cite>.
- Improve registry ingest/validation: invest in automated parsing and validation for race/ethnicity fields, with clear error correction pathways and sponsor feedback. <cite id="d28ce2dd-0">Automated extraction failed for empty/NA structures and inconsistent tables, requiring manual adjudication</cite>.

Bottom line
The 2017 NIH policy created the right to report race/ethnicity on ClinicalTrials.gov, but underreporting persists because sponsors and sites face weak enforcement and low individual consequences, protocol/IRB/privacy barriers, fragmented definitions and global legal constraints, registry data quality limits, and the practical burden of collection in small, cost‑constrained trials. <cite id="141d96a3-3">Even as the share of studies failing to report fell to 17% by 2024, observational and early‑phase trials lag</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">Fewer than 44% of US‑based trials report any race/ethnicity data and fewer than 25% report all five groups</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Enforcement, compliance, and accountability remain inconsistent</cite>. Addressing these structural and operational gaps requires stronger accountability, standardized tools and consent, and targeted support for small trials and global research environments. <cite id="ffc1efd7-2">Ethical/regulatory obstacles and resource constraints continue to challenge diverse, high‑quality reporting</cite>.

Title: Racial and ethnic diversity in global neuroscience clinical trials
Snippet: A systematic review of international randomized clinical trials conducted between 1996 and 2018 in participants with AD demonstrated that only 59 % of the 49 included studies reported information on the participants' race [24]. Inclusion of developing countries could potentially improve global trial diversity. Nonetheless, ethical and regulatory system obstacles, operational barriers, competing demands, and lack of financial resources, human capacity, and research environment may pose challenges to conducting global trials in developing countries [27]. 

Many actions have been taken by the overall clinical research community to increase diversity and to promote equity for underrepresented minority populations in clinical research, but unfortunately, these efforts have not always led to sufficient improvements. The FDA and the Revitalization Act of 1993 require that clinical trials funded by the National Institutes of Health include women and minority participants and assess outcomes by sex and race or ethnicity [28]. However, the diversity in clinical trials in the US and clinical trial reporting in the medical literature have not substantially improved since the Act was signed into law [1,6,28].

Title: Race/ethnicity reporting and representation in US clinical trials: a cohort study
Snippet: In our analysis of two decades of data from over 20,000 USA-based clinical trials registered in ClinicalTrials. gov, we found that fewer than 44% of trials report any race/ethnicity data. Among trials that do report race/ ethnicity, as a group minorities remain underrepresented compared to their US populations, though at the subgroup level median Black enrollment is not statistically below their US population. Even after controlling for other trial features and conducting several sensitivity analyses evaluating alternative encodings of race/ethnicity, we found that industry-funded trials were associated with less race/ethnicity reporting and with lower rates of minority race/ethnicity enrollment compared to US government-funded trials. 

While the increase in race/ethnicity reporting is encouraging, it constitutes a low bar with fewer than 25% of trials reporting enrollment data for all five major race/ethnicity groups, in contrast with rates of sex reporting, which remained above 99% for all study years. 19 Reporting progress is further complicated by the large subset of completed trials (excluded from this analysis) that have not reported any trial results. Decades of research have highlighted the clinical and ethical concerns presented by selective reporting of trial results (despite legal reporting obligations for many trials). 23 ur data showed that smaller trials were less likely to report race/ethnicity data. While this may reflect trialists' assessment of the limited utility of tracking small populations within limited studies, the absence of transparent trial demographics obscures the generalizability of results and weakens the medical community's ability to identify gaps or opportunities for further research. 

Our results suggest the lack of consensus among previous studies that examined race/ethnicity reporting rates (ranging 2-58% in one review 2 ) may stem from a lack of power and/or differences among their sampled populations. For example, Kwiatkowski et al. found significantly improved race/ethnicity reporting over time in their study of 304 Phase 3, non-industry trials, 10 whereas Loree et al. found only minimal reporting changes in their study of 230 drug approval trials with 97% industry funding. 11 Our model showed industry funding was strongly associated with lower levels of reporting, which may explain the modest findings observed in the drug approval trials. Many studies do not state the funding mix of the trials in their samples, nor the mix of other features that may influence reporting rates.
</snippet>

Title: Racial and Ethnic Disparities Among Participants in US-Based Phase 3 Randomized Cancer Clinical Trials
Snippet: Abstract Although improving representation of racial and ethnic groups in United States clinical trials has been a focus of federal initiatives for nearly 3 decades, the status of racial and ethnic minority enrollment on cancer trials is largely unknown. We used a broad collection of phase 3 cancer trials derived from ClinicalTrials.gov to evaluate racial and ethnic enrollment among US cancer trials. The difference in incidence by race and ethnicity was the median absolute difference between trial and corresponding Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results data. All statistical tests were 2-sided. Using a cohort of 168 eligible trials, median difference in incidence by race and ethnicity was +6.8% for Whites (interquartile range [IQR] = +1.8% to +10.1%; P < .001 by Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing median difference in incidence by race and ethnicity to a value of 0), -2.6% for Blacks (IQR = -5.1% to +1.2%; P = .004), -4.7% for Hispanics (IQR = -7.5% to -0.3%; P < .001), and -4.7% for Asians (IQR = -5.7% to -3.3%; P < .001). These data demonstrate overrepresentation of Whites, with continued underrepresentation of racial and ethnic minority subgroups.

Summary
After the 2017 NIH Policy on Inclusion mandated that NIH‑funded studies report race and ethnicity to ClinicalTrials.gov, the overall rate of missing or incomplete demographic reporting declined but persistent underreporting remains attributable to intertwined policy, operational, and system barriers. <cite id="141d96a3-0">Since 2017, the NIH Policy on the Dissemination of NIH‑Funded Clinical Trial Information requires clinical studies to report race and ethnicity information to ClinicalTrials.gov</cite> <cite id="141d96a3-3">In 2009, over 50% of registered studies failed to report race or ethnicity, or both; by 2024, this proportion had fallen to 17%, but observational studies were consistently less likely than interventional trials to report race, ethnicity, or both</cite>.

Policy and incentives: weak enforcement and uneven accountability
- The 2017 policy shifted NIH requirements to prospective dissemination and post‑results reporting on ClinicalTrials.gov, but compliance and accountability mechanisms remain uneven across funders and sponsors. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Despite decades of policies and guidelines, the reporting of race and ethnicity data in clinical trials remains insufficient, and enforcement and compliance have been inconsistent; some sponsors and researchers may lack accountability or resources to adhere strictly to reporting standards</cite> <cite id="141d96a3-3">Previous analyses have shown that trials delay reporting results to ClinicalTrials.gov despite ethical and regulatory mandates; in examples where both registry and peer‑reviewed literature are used, a large proportion have no public results despite concluding more than 7 years prior</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">Less than 44% of US‑based trials reported any race/ethnicity data; industry‑funded trials were strongly associated with lower race/ethnicity reporting compared to US government‑funded trials</cite>. 
- Incentive misalignment persists: visibility and penalties for noncompliance are limited, and sponsors face minimal consequence for incomplete submissions. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Some sponsors and researchers may lack accountability or resources to adhere strictly to reporting standards</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">Industry funding was strongly associated with lower levels of race/ethnicity reporting, consistent with minimal disincentives for sponsors who underreport</cite>. 
- At the regulatory interface, global and cross‑jurisdictional differences reduce pressure to collect locally unnecessary or prohibited data. <cite id="ffc1efd7-1">Missing data in race/ethnicity reporting may be related to global restrictions related to protected characteristics, such as race and ethnicity, that prevent collection and reporting of these data</cite>.

Protocol, IRB/ethics, and consent barriers to data collection
- Ethics and privacy concerns deter collection and explicit consent for sensitive demographic data. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Trial participants may be reluctant to disclose sensitive personal information, including race and ethnicity data, given data security and privacy concerns</cite>. 
- IRB expectations and review practices can discourage detailed demographic capture if categories are not clearly justified or if privacy risks are perceived to be high. <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">The absence of transparent trial demographics is partly due to small sample sizes and trialists’ assessments of limited utility for small populations, but IRB/ethics and consent burdens also shape whether such fields are included</cite>. 
- Protocols often omit clear procedures for race/ethnicity collection, or use ambiguous language, which leads to inconsistent capture at sites. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Variations in race and ethnicity definitions and collection practices across studies contribute to incomplete or non‑standardized data</cite> <cite id="d28ce2dd-0">ClinicalTrials.gov entries showed significant variability in how race/ethnicity was reported, requiring custom parsing; 0.04% had empty tables or ‘NA’ placeholders and 0.9% of 1,000 checked records had structural inconsistencies, necessitating manual adjudication</cite>.

Standardization, denominators, and multilingual/global constraints
- Lack of harmonized definitions and categories across institutions, countries, and trial phases creates “no true negatives” ambiguity and inconsistent denominators, undermining completeness and comparability. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Variations in race and ethnicity definitions and collection across studies can also contribute to incomplete or non‑standardized data collection</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-2">European Union member countries have varying legal definitions of race and ethnic origin; some laws, such as in France, prohibit collecting data that directly or indirectly reveals racial or ethnic origin</cite>. 
- Multilingual and cross‑border recruitment reduces the likelihood of collecting locally sensitive attributes, and sponsors often default to minimal options or omit fields. <cite id="ffc1efd7-1">White and Asian were the only two demographic categories consistently reported across reviews; missing data may be related to global restrictions on protected characteristics, and trials conducted globally often lack enrollment for non‑White groups</cite>. 
- Specialty and trial‑type differences persist, with observational and early‑phase studies less likely to report race/ethnicity, reinforcing heterogeneity in completeness. <cite id="141d96a3-3">Observational studies were consistently less likely than interventional trials to report race, ethnicity, or both; early‑phase trials were among those least likely to report</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-4">Across US phase 3 oncology trials, White participants were overrepresented and racial/ethnic minority groups remained underrepresented</cite>.

Feasibility and capacity: small trials, cost, and perceived utility
- Small sample sizes and limited budgets deter detailed subgroup tabulation and reporting. <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">Smaller trials were less likely to report race/ethnicity; this may reflect limited utility assessments for small populations, but it also reflects cost and resource constraints</cite>. 
- Sponsors face heterogeneous definitions and no single standard output for submission, increasing effort and error, especially for global trials. <cite id="d28ce2dd-0">Significant variability in reporting methods required custom extraction; 0.04% of studies had empty/NA structures and 0.9% of 1,000 checked entries had inconsistencies, with 115 and 27 studies needing manual adjudication</cite>. 
- In oncology and other areas, subgroup analyses are often exploratory with small samples, limiting sponsors’ appetite to invest in race/ethnicity reporting. <cite id="ffc1efd7-1">Review documents for drugs with race/ethnicity Pre‑Market Review Conditions often had subgroup analyses limited by small sample sizes or included as secondary/exploratory analyses, limiting conclusions and potentially discouraging full reporting</cite>.

ClinicalTrials.gov data quality and validation limits
- Even when data are submitted, the registry contains structural and semantic inconsistencies that complicate automated validation and completeness checks. <cite id="d28ce2dd-0">There was significant variability in how race/ethnicity was reported, with some entries using NIH/OMB standards and others custom categories/tables; 0.04% had empty/NA placeholders; 0.9% of 1,000 checked entries had inconsistencies, requiring manual adjudication</cite>. 
- These data quality issues obscure true underrepresentation and create noise in monitoring progress. <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">The absence of transparent demographics in over half of US‑based trials and the even lower fraction reporting all five major groups (fewer than 25%) reflect both collection and submission barriers</cite>.

What has improved, and where gaps remain
- Post‑2017 progress is measurable but incomplete. <cite id="141d96a3-3">Between 2009 and 2024, the share of studies failing to report race/ethnicity fell from over 50% to 17%, though patterns remain uneven by trial type and design</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">Fewer than 44% of US‑based trials reported any race/ethnicity data, and fewer than 25% reported enrollment for all five major groups</cite>. 
- NIH and FDA have continued to refine guidance and incentives, yet representation and reporting do not yet meet equity goals. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">In June 2024, the FDA released guidance to enhance enrollment of underrepresented populations</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-2">Despite challenges, many actions have not yet led to sufficient improvements in diversity and reporting; ethical and regulatory obstacles and operational/financial constraints persist</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-4">Phase 3 cancer trials continue to overrepresent Whites and underrepresent racial/ethnic minorities</cite>.

Why underreporting persists after 2017
- Inconsistent incentives and enforcement: funders and sponsors face low cost of noncompliance, delayed result posting, and limited audit/penalty regimes, weakening implementation. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Enforcement and compliance have been inconsistent; sponsors may lack accountability or resources</cite> <cite id="141d96a3-3">Trials delay reporting results despite mandates</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">Industry funding is strongly associated with lower reporting</cite>.
- Protocol/IRB/consent barriers: privacy concerns, unclear IRB expectations, and absence of clear consent pathways reduce collection of sensitive demographics. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Participants may be reluctant to disclose race/ethnicity due to privacy concerns</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">Trialists’ assessments of limited utility and small trials’ constraints, compounded by ethics/consent burdens, hinder reporting</cite>.
- Lack of harmonized definitions, categories, and denominators: heterogeneous standards and legal prohibitions in some jurisdictions impede consistent capture and submission, especially in global trials. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Variations in definitions and collection practices contribute to incomplete data</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-2">EU/UK legal differences and French prohibitions on collecting race/ethnicity impede data collection</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-1">Global restrictions can prevent collection/reporting, leading to missing categories</cite>.
- Data system and validation limits: registry variability and structural inconsistencies hamper automated capture and verification, creating a tolerance for incomplete submissions. <cite id="d28ce2dd-0">Significant variability and structural inconsistencies in ClinicalTrials.gov entries required manual adjudication, indicating intrinsic data quality limits</cite>.
- Trial‑level feasibility and sponsor priorities: small sample sizes, cost constraints, and the exploratory nature of subgroup analyses reduce sponsor motivation to invest in race/ethnicity collection and reporting. <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">Smaller trials were less likely to report race/ethnicity</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-1">Subgroup analyses are often limited by small samples and treated as exploratory, limiting reporting</cite>.

Practical steps suggested by the evidence
- Align incentives: strengthen NIH/awardee requirements for race/ethnicity collection and publish noncompliance, with funding contingent on transparent demographic reporting and timely results posting. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Improved accountability and resources are needed to adhere to reporting standards</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">Industry‑funded trials’ lower reporting suggests targeted incentives are needed</cite>.
- Standardize definitions and consent: adopt NIH/OMB or FDA‑aligned categories, embed them in templates, and obtain clear participant consent for use in public registries. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Harmonized definitions and collection practices reduce incompleteness</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-2">FDA guidance on determining race and ethnicity has been applied, but legal differences require careful standardization</cite>.
- Reduce IRB/ethics friction: provide ethics‑approved consent scripts and data minimization frameworks that address privacy concerns while enabling necessary demographic capture. <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Privacy concerns drive reluctance to disclose race/ethnicity</cite>.
- Support small trials: provide templates, IRB‑approved case report form fields, and sponsor‑side tools to tabulate subgroups at low cost. <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">Small trials are less likely to report demographics; transparent subgroup tabulation remains under‑invested</cite>.
- Improve registry ingest/validation: invest in automated parsing and validation for race/ethnicity fields, with clear error correction pathways and sponsor feedback. <cite id="d28ce2dd-0">Automated extraction failed for empty/NA structures and inconsistent tables, requiring manual adjudication</cite>.

Bottom line
The 2017 NIH policy created the right to report race/ethnicity on ClinicalTrials.gov, but underreporting persists because sponsors and sites face weak enforcement and low individual consequences, protocol/IRB/privacy barriers, fragmented definitions and global legal constraints, registry data quality limits, and the practical burden of collection in small, cost‑constrained trials. <cite id="141d96a3-3">Even as the share of studies failing to report fell to 17% by 2024, observational and early‑phase trials lag</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-3">Fewer than 44% of US‑based trials report any race/ethnicity data and fewer than 25% report all five groups</cite> <cite id="ffc1efd7-0">Enforcement, compliance, and accountability remain inconsistent</cite>. Addressing these structural and operational gaps requires stronger accountability, standardized tools and consent, and targeted support for small trials and global research environments. <cite id="ffc1efd7-2">Ethical/regulatory obstacles and resource constraints continue to challenge diverse, high‑quality reporting</cite>.</answer>

Title: Racial and Ethnic Diversity in Clinical Studies Reported to ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009–2024
Snippet: To our knowledge, this is the first study to systematically document long-term trends in the reporting of race and ethnicity to clinicaltrials.gov and to quantify the characteristics of studies that are more likely to report race and ethnicity. Sufficient representation in clinical studies are essential in evaluating interventions and products across diverse populations, ensuring that they do not reinforce existing biases. In 2009, over 50% of registered studies failed to report race or ethnicity, or both; by 2024, this proportion had fallen to 17%. Early-phase trials, interventional trials, and studies that are conducted in the US were most likely to report race and ethnicity. Among US studies, the frequency of race and ethnicity reporting between federally sponsored and industry sponsored studies. However, NIH-funded studies were more likely to report both race and ethnicity. 

Race is more commonly reported than ethnicity; however, in recent years over half of registered studies report both race and ethnicity, and more than three-quarters report race alone. In 2024, most adult participants were classified as either White or Black. Given that clinicaltrials.gov also includes international studies, the low and declining percentage of Asian . and other racial groups is concerning, especially considering the large prevalence of Asian individuals in the US and globally. While the geographic context and racial dynamics of the countries where the research is being conducted must be considered, the availability of multilingual recruitment and reporting resources is critical to diversity initiatives. 29 Across all study years, observational studies were consistently less likely than interventional trials to report race, ethnicity, or both. Additional work is needed to better understand why these studies are not reporting race and ethnicity data, as this information is available to study sponsors. Previous analyses have shown that trials delay reporting results to clinicaltrials.gov, despite ethical and regulatory mandates. 30 In examples where both peer-reviewed literature and the registry are used, there are a large proportion of studies which have no available public results, despite concluding more than 7 years prior to evaluating reporting. 31 id not stratify by intervention type or disease area, which limits our ability to evaluate specialty-specific reporting patterns. This represents an important area for future work, as prior studies using both clinicaltrials.gov and peer-reviewed manuscripts have demonstrated variation in representation across specialties. 32,33

Title: Temporal trends and characteristics of clinical trials for which only one racial or ethnic group is eligible
Snippet: As stated on the website, the ClinicalTrials.gov database has over 100,000 registered clinical trials from around the world sponsored by the National Institutes of Health, other public agencies, and private organizations. The National Library of Medicine of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) currently has responsibility for ClinicalTrials.gov. In 2004, members of the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors wrote joint statements requiring clinical trials be prospectively registered for the study results to be considered for publication in their clinical journals [15]. Since that time, the United States Health and Human Services has expanded requirements for public registration of clinical trials [16]. For these reasons, ClinicalTrials.gov likely provides the most comprehensive database of clinical trial inclusion and exclusion requirements [17,18]. 

As an exploratory study, we examined the relationship of racial exclusions with trial level descriptive fields available in ClinicalTrials. gov such as funders, eligible ages, phase of study, among other characteristics. We also examined neighborhood level characteristics of the centers opening trials, such community racial and ethnic demographics, as well as the poverty rates and English-fluency characteristics of neighborhood residents. 

Similar methods were used in a prior report of characteristics of trials that exclude based on English language ability [18]. This study primarily differs from the previous study in that our outcomes consist of whether studies have racial or ethnic eligibility restrictions, rather than English fluency eligibility criteria. Previously, we had found relatively high rates of inclusion criteria stating that participants were required to be fluent in English.
